To collect necessary spatial and temporal information on these sundials, a citizen science initiative could be implemented, addressing research inquiries while promoting science education among the general public. This concept has been proposed as a framework, referred to as the Suryakala-Nusantara program, to explore sundials through citizen science methods.

This research focuses on an integrated data and energy transmission network, which incorporates D2D communication. This hybrid network allows a central hub to transfer data and electricity to remote locations, while also facilitating D2D communication and energy transfer between end devices. This integrated system addresses the challenge of a lack of power infrastructure in remote areas by utilizing the existing electrical network. A key challenge in this hybrid network is managing cochannel interference. To minimize this interference, we propose an intelligent reflecting surface (IRS) optimization framework. This framework uses convex optimization to maximize the spectral efficiency of the network by controlling the IRS reflections to maximize the signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio. To reduce computational complexity, we also develop a suboptimal algorithm based on alternating optimization. Simulations demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework, showing significant improvements in spectral efficiency, with gains of up to 80% and 90% over traditional interference management methods.

The surge in telework needs has highlighted the potential benefits of fully
automating and controlling experiments remotely. This work presents the technical
advancements of creating a two-dimensional LDV measurement system using a single-
point LDV system via a remotely controllable and automated setup. The document's
aim is to expedite the development of similar setups for this kind of application,
which is highly versatile and can be applied to various scenarios including both
air-based acoustic signal-driven samples and mechanically induced samples.

The effectiveness of programmable electrostatic phase plates is subject to debate 
given their varying suitability for particular applications. Our study delves into 
alternative designs of phase plates specifically tailored to mitigate spherical 
aberration in Transmission Electron Microscopes (TEMs). Through numerical analysis, 
we investigate the potential for a phase plate to attain quasi-optimal electron 
distribution on the detector across various conditions. Furthermore, we examine 
the feasibility of designing a retractable electrostatic phase plate that can 
switch between correcting spherical aberration and generating a diffraction 
pattern using TEM's astigmatism, without the need for specimen charging control.

The success of data-driven dialogue models heavily relies on their ability to accurately encode user input to generate relevant and effective responses. While it is common to evaluate the generated text for its semantic and syntactic quality, the underlying representation of this encoding is often overlooked, which can hinder the model's performance in anticipating the next utterance. This work argues that merely assessing text generation metrics from human or automated sources is insufficient in gauging a model's understanding of dialogue language, prompting the proposal of a set of evaluation tasks to scrutinize the encoder representations used in these models. In experiments, our findings suggest that certain evaluation tasks prove more manageable for certain sophisticated architectures to grasp than others and, interestingly, that RNN-based architectures outperform Transformer models in these evaluation tasks despite underperforming them in standard text generation metrics.

Deep learning methods for LiDAR data analysis have revolutionized 3D place recognition in autonomous vehicles by improving accuracy and robustness. However, extracting effective local features from LiDAR scans remains a challenge. To address this issue, this research introduces a novel, multi-local-feature-extraction deep learning model called AttDLNet, which leverages attention mechanisms to selectively emphasize salient local features from point clouds. By combining local and global descriptors using a global attention mechanism, AttDLNet enhances matching stability. The model is tested and evaluated on the KITTI dataset, with results showing improved performance and efficiency compared to existing methods.

Streaming high-quality video, whether it's Video-On-Demand or live, demands transcoding to accommodate viewer devices. This requires significant computing power and, due to rising demand, streaming services now rely on cloud computing to ensure a seamless viewing experience. Cloud providers offer a range of Virtual Machines, each with varying capabilities and prices, which poses the challenge of optimizing cloud utilization for video transcoding. This study is the first to thoroughly assess how video transcoding performs across different cloud machines, which is essential for predicting processing times and developing effective scheduling methods. Based on this analysis and the cost variability of cloud machines, the research provides a model that helps evaluate the suitability of each cloud machine for different transcoding tasks. This model can provide resource provisioning with the best balance of performance and cost, thus enhancing the efficient use of cloud services for video streaming.

We have derived a semi-analytical formula for the dynamic density-density correlation of massless Dirac electrons in doped graphene, which is applicable at finite temperatures. Our calculation builds on Keldysh contour techniques and involves a complex thermal width in the dispersion relation. A thorough analysis of the correlation function is presented, revealing a Lorentzian shape that is influenced by the thermal width and chemical potential. The influence of temperature and doping on the correlation function is examined in detail. Furthermore, we have calculated the total density-density correlation function, considering the parabolic shape of the density of states in graphene. Additionally, we have investigated the thermal broadening of the chemical potential-induced shift and its impact on the correlation function. A numerical evaluation of the sum over the momentum space contributes to the total density-density correlation function is performed. This enables us to predict the electronic specific heat for doping levels that do not intersect the Dirac points.

Continuous speech leads to consistent prosody patterns, yet current speech synthesis models often disregard context. These systems fall short when it comes to producing high-quality paragraphs, necessitating a system that integrates contextual elements. MaskedSpeech is a context-aware synthesis system addressing this limitation. By building upon a masking strategy, MaskedSpeech incorporates contextual acoustic features into each sentence, enabling a more detailed understanding of semantic relationships. Additionally, cross-sentence coarse-grained features aid in the development of a natural prosody. Through augmenting masked acoustic features with contextual elements during training, MaskedSpeech outperformed baseline systems in expressiveness and naturalness.

We provide explicit definitions for the spectral and orbital stability of solitary waves in a model that includes a Klein-Gordon equation and an anharmonic oscillator. We also conduct a comprehensive analysis of the linearized equation's spectrum at the solitary wave state.

Q-ball studies in a single symmetry theory are common, yet the field can be more expansive, allowing for the examination of theories featuring multiple symmetries in a more general context. In this paper, we explore this broader scenario, analyzing both the standard and advanced limits within this theoretical framework and identifying essential conditions for existence in the more complex scenarios. Additionally, we identify a previously unexamined Q-ball state, which we term 'cored', and demonstrate that it could possess stability under specific conditions; a further area for further research in this field.

We investigated a cyclic universe containing holographic dark energy with different infrared cutoffs, excluding the Big Rip singularity. The study reveals that, in the absence of interaction between the cosmos sectors, the HDE model using the Hubble radius cutoff behaves like a cosmological constant within cyclic cosmology. Furthermore, we discovered that cyclic patterns of contraction and expansion may occur for both interacting and non-interacting universes, provided that the Granda-Oliveros cutoff is selected for the HDE's energy density.

Gnutzmann and Smilansky previously developed a formula for the bond scattering matrix of a graph using a Hermitian matrix, for which an alternative proof has been devised, employing a method related to the zeta function of a graph. Furthermore, the formula has been broadened to cover regular coverings of graphs, and a novel 'L-function' concept for graphs has been defined, yielding a determinant expression. This has a corresponding outcome where the extended Gnutzmann and Smilansky formula can be represented by the graph's 'L-functions'.

We derive new conclusions regarding the additive Galois module properties of specific wildly ramified finite non-abelian extensions of Q. Notably, in cases where K/Q is a Galois extension with a Galois group isomorphic to A4, S4 or A5, we determine the ramified prime numbers, determine the ramified primes' maximal ramification properties, and explicitly define the embedding of the Galois group into the automorphism group of the rational function field over Q with respect to a specific set of variables.

In experiments involving particle collisions, identifying neutral long-lived particles relies on finding decay products that aren't immediately contained within the detector or result in missing energy. Typically, a hadronic decay like $\pi^0$ is used as a reference point for such measurements. However, if these particles decay into photons, determining their origin is more challenging due to potential contributions from other processes. Based on a specific decay mode, $B \rightarrow K (\text{AXION}) \gamma$, we use statistical methods to distinguish a scenario where the axion is detectable from a scenario where it isn't, using a combination of experimental data and theoretical predictions with consideration of various effects such as form factors and photon polarization. Specifically, we analyze two cases: one where the absence of certain decay modes indicates the presence of a neutral long-lived particle, and one where a neutral long-lived particle cannot be identified due to an overlapping bound of decay modes attributed to another cause. Using this approach, we estimate the number of event scenarios that could lead to a given $B$-decays data set with a certain distribution of multiplicities of certain hadronic particles in the final state. Furthermore, we extract from this a suppression factor of approximately $10^3$ in multiplicities of certain hadronic final states in $B$-decays that could contain a neutral long-lived particle, compared to standard QCD predictions.

This study provides a detailed examination of the potential inaccuracies in
the output of contextualized language models when analyzing diachronic semantic
shifts in word meanings. We present an enhanced ensemble method that surpasses
earlier contextualized approaches and apply it to investigate the levels of
semantic change in English vocabulary over the course of 5 decades. Our
results show that contextualized methods may inaccurately predict significant
change in words with little to no actual semantic evolution, or whose
status remains unclear. These difficult cases are scrutinized, along with
suggested categorizations, to better understand the challenges. We also
explore potential explanations for these difficulties, including issues with
ambiguity, negation, and hypothetical scenarios. Moreover, we highlight the
importance of distinguishing between different types of difficult cases and
contemplate avenues for further research in this area.

Active galactic nuclei (AGNs) can provide information about the fundamental properties of ultralight bosons, which could potentially explain 95% of dark matter. By linking the maximum and minimum spin states of a accreting black hole with the rate at which a boson is radiated, we can determine the boson's mass and other characteristics. A key factor in this analysis is the "event horizon," the boundary beyond which nothing, including light, can escape from a black hole's gravitational pull. To calculate the mass of an ultralight boson, we need to know the minimum spin state of a black hole with a mass that corresponds to the event horizon of a spinning black hole. Quasars, which are the most spin-intensive AGNs, offer the best hope of finding this information. By looking at the relationship between the spin states of heavy quasars and assuming that their spin can be up to 0.99, we can calculate the mass of an ultralight boson to be around 10^-23 GeV, a value that is consistent with the parameters required by Higgsian dark matter. Additionally, we can also determine the maximum possible number of ultralight boson masses and we find that, assuming the minimum spin state of a heavy quasars is 0.99, there can be up to 10^5 different ultralight boson masses, each corresponding to a specific spin state and black hole mass combination.

A distinctive feature of neural development is the rhythmic shifting of cell nuclei
between the upper and lower layers of the neuroepithelial tissue as interkinetic nuclear
migration (IKNM) unfolds. In this study, we utilize extended, high-speed light-sheet imaging
and sophisticated analysis methods in the retina of zebrafish to gain insights into the
spatial behavior of nuclei during their migration towards specific destinations.
Our research indicates that the speed of nuclei varies depending on the layer they are
in, with faster movement occurring in the lower layer, and that this difference in speed
may result in uneven movement rates across different layers due to the unique geometry
of these layers. Our data also reveal that the orientation of nuclei as they migrate
is random and unrelated to their ultimate destination. Notably, our findings challenge
the widely held hypothesis that the orientation of nuclei during IKNM is directionally
aligned. Instead, we propose a more flexible concept, where specific orientations only
become apparent when considering the long-term cumulative effects of migration across
the entire neuroepithelial domain. Our discovery that nuclei exhibit random behavior
during migration also opens up intriguing possibilities for the occurrence of stochastic
events, such as stroke or mechanical disruption, affecting IKNM patterns.

In various image processing tasks, including video compressed sensing and color image demosaicing, images must be separated from coded measurements that represent their superposition. Real-world code patterns, which are often non-negative, systematically structured and non-Gaussian, can impede reconstruction performance due to their non-ideal coherence properties. This research addresses this challenge by developing optimized code patterns that minimize the coherence of the sensing matrix and signal representation matrix combination, taking into consideration their inherent structural properties, specifically non-negativity, block-diagonal structure, and circular shifting, which are particularly beneficial for certain compressed sensing architectures, facilitating accurate and seamless reconstruction of compressed images.

We've developed a comprehensive hydrodynamic theory that applies to polar active fluids in the presence of randomly distributed inclusions, and our model demonstrates the possibility of overcoming these obstructions to maintain a non-zero overall speed. Contrary to previous research, the dynamics of this specific class of active matter cannot be accurately captured using simplified hydrodynamic models when the spatial environment is two-dimensional up to five-dimensional space; however, we were able to derive precise, dimension-dependent scaling parameters for these dimensions.

Researchers within the same institution often rely on their institutional email as their primary means of communication. Due to their accessibility and private data storage, these emails are vulnerable to cyber threats and can serve as lucrative targets. Our proposed approach aims to examine research institutions' internal communication networks for potential security breaches. Initially, we gathered and analyzed email data from multiple research institutions, including three in Spain and one in Portugal. We applied an SEIR complex network dynamics model to simulate and assess the vulnerability of these networks. Our results indicated that a significant proportion of email accounts have experienced security breaches, while more than 90% of network nodes exhibit susceptibility to cyber threats. Our research can facilitate the enhancement of email account security for research institutions, while also opening up avenues for further exploration in the realm of communication security. Due to confidentiality considerations, we cannot disclose the source from which we acquired the communication network data, as this would reveal sensitive information.

Inspired by the pseudogap phenomenon in cuprates, we propose a new idea, 
the concept of an "exceptional" van Hove singularity, where a strong 
electron interaction fragments a continuous Fermi surface into disjoint regions. 
We identify this singularity with the merging of two separated Fermi surface 
segments, and demonstrate that it is close to a van Hove singularity, 
reaching it by adjusting a material parameter affecting its dispersion. 
We assert that, in the broader family of cuprate materials, 
the onset of pseudogap is attainable solely through inducing this exceptional 
van Hove singularity, and that this results in a distinct Lifshitz 
transition distinguished by heightened heat capacity and a nematic susceptibility, 
both consistent with empirical observations.

This paper details a specialized apparatus built for use in Aberdeen Tunnel's laboratory in Hong Kong. The laboratory is uniquely situated to study spallation neutrons produced by cosmic-ray muons with 611 meters of water equivalent in depth. The apparatus consists of six layers of horizontal plastic-scintillator detectors that pinpoint the direction and location of incoming muons. Between these layers, a neutron sensor filled with 650 kilograms of liquid scintillator containing a gadolinium dopant significantly enhances detection efficiency of the produced spallation neutrons. Additionally, we discuss the performance characteristics of this apparatus.

Ground-based observations of planetary movements are crucial in validating the findings of space-based missions like Kepler and TESS. Although these missions show that planets are widespread, the success of these missions relies heavily on the use of transit photometry and ground-based radial velocity surveys to determine the physical properties of these celestial bodies. The TESS telescope is capable of identifying planets around bright nearby stars, which are ideal candidates for follow-up observations. We propose the TESS-Keck Survey to investigate various properties of these exoplanets. Utilizing 100 nights on the Keck/HIRES, the survey's primary objectives include analyzing how the compositions of rocky worlds are determined by the temperature conditions on their host stars, as well as identifying potential mini-Neptunes that can be studied in detail by missions like James Webb Space Telescope and Hubble Space Telescope. Additionally, the survey aims to validate the findings of TESS by discovering and characterizing the planets it has identified around the closest seventh magnitude or brighter stars. The target selection involves a multi-criteria approach to select the most suitable candidates for further analysis using their TESS light curves, spectral types, and abundance levels. Ultimately, the targets chosen demonstrate the capabilities of TESS to detect and identify planets around stars similar to the Sun, which is consistent with previous expectations.

The growth of Information Technology has significantly altered how information is shared, making it necessary to convert printed documents into digital formats.  There has been an increase in fraudulent activities lately.  To prevent such account-related fraud, a system was devised which employs ID card extraction via OCR and NLP for verification purposes.  Optical Character Recognition, a technology that enables the conversion of images to text, was used to convert the ID card image into text.  This text was then processed using Natural Language Processing to extract the information in the desired format suitable for comparison with the ID card holder's actual details.  When the extracted data from the ID card does not match the actual details, the system detects anomalies.  The ID card extraction system was tested using a dataset consisting of 3000 ID card images and was found to be effective in accurately extracting the necessary information.

Quantum harmonic oscillators were computationally analyzed in their ground state with either steady-state driving forces varying in intensity or driving forces that changed over time. Calculations of position expectations were carried out for multiple scenarios of mass, angular frequency, and the lambda parameter in both cases. Constant driving led to coherent states, with theoretical predictions closely matched by both simulation approaches. A discrete-time lattice Metropolis algorithm was used to evaluate the imaginary time path integral for these simulations.

The Yarkovsky-O'Keefe-Radzievskii-Paddack effect significantly impacts the rotational states of small asteroids by exerting a net torque resulting from solar radiation reflected and re-emitted by the surface. As a consequence of this phenomenon, the rotation period of an asteroid gradually changes, which can be best measured through light curves as the phase shift accumulates over time in a quadratic manner. To study this effect in detail, researchers collected archived data and conducted new photometric observations for asteroids 1992 SK, Geographos, and Toro, before utilizing them in a light curve inversion framework to estimate their physical properties and rotation acceleration. The findings indicate that the YORP effect is responsible for the observed acceleration in rotation rates of 1992 SK and Geographos, with estimated increases in their rotation periods in approximately 4.5 years and 5.4 years respectively. In contrast, the data collected for Toro did not align with the expected YORP acceleration, which could be attributed to external forces interfering with its irregular rotation dynamics.

The youth are increasingly relying on Instagram as a source of information, with political figures leveraging the platform to disseminate opinions and agendas. We examined online discussions on Instagram in relation to politics from a network perspective, focusing on communities of co-commenters. Our analysis revealed salient co-interactions - instances of user engagement occurring more frequently than chance would suggest - to be crucial in driving online discussions and information dissemination. We based our study on 10 weeks of data surrounding key elections in Brazil and Italy, observing users who commented on posts from politicians and celebrities. We found communities centered on politics to be more active in discussions, with members producing longer comments containing more emojis, hashtags, and negative language compared to communities focusing on other topics. Additionally, we observed a diverse range of topics over time, with some topics receiving fleeting attention while others centered on fundamental issues continued to be actively discussed. Communities involved in politics displayed dynamic characteristics, with new users continuously emerging to contribute their perspectives. We found the likelihood of new users joining a community to be lower for politics than other topics, with some political discussions showing resilience in adaptation. Communities centered on politics demonstrated distinct patterns in pre-election periods, with a shift in topic focus occurring right before voting day.

We show that any subgroup of homeomorphisms of a compact surface that fix the boundary, whose action within the surface's interior is highly transitive, cannot be topologically compact when using the compact-open topology's inherited structure.

By observing local star populations in the ultraviolet, we can gather details about how hydrogen, helium, and metal content vary in M-dwarfs. To do this for The M-dwarf Ultraviolet Spectroscopic Sample, we employed a combination of methods to accurately determine the stellar parameters (temperature, surface gravity, and metal content) for each star. The temperature measurements came from GALEX, GLoBAL, and Infrared Photometry, while surface gravities were calculated using mass estimates based on parallax and radius measurements. We also considered the metal content of nearby associations, and ultimately calculated the metal content of the sample stars using a weighted average. The temperature range for the sample stars is 3,600 to 4,100 K, and the metal contents are between -0.6 and +0.5 in [Fe/H]. The study finds that the temperature range for M-dwarfs in the solar neighborhood is narrower than previously estimated and that the metal contents of M-dwarfs with high surface densities are lower than those in similar mass G-dwarfs.

Confining modes at the edge, known as line waves, can propagate on the boundary between two specially designed electromagnetic interfaces that maintain mirror symmetry properties.
Studies have previously analyzed line waves in theory and in practice, revealing their occurrence at both microwave and terahertz frequencies.
It has also been demonstrated that these waves can occur when there's a sudden change from a negative to a positive symmetric resistance and uniform surface reactance present.
Characteristics of line waves include highly confineable mode propagation, polarization dependent on direction, and unique localized field enhancements.
A new study proposes a graphene patch structure, showing that the line waves produced can operate in the optical range.
The design involves a graphene surface integrated with an epsilon near zero substrate, which considers the effects of both dual and uniform reactances.
However, this work specifically focuses on utilizing line waves in dual reactance scenarios.

Although a key function in database management, query evaluation classification lacks comprehensive guidelines when dealing with self-joined queries. Our investigation aims to bridge this knowledge gap by examining how self-joins impact the complexity of enumerating database results, building on existing research. By extending two known categories of classification to incorporate self-joined queries with respect to efficiency, this study provides an in-depth analysis and illustrates potential enumeration strategies using self-joins. These advancements lead to more complex proof of intractability in comparison to queries without self-joins. Additionally, this study introduces an existing method to prove intractability in the presence of self-joins and sets criteria for both feasible and infeasible queries with limited complexity, providing answers for low-arity queries and those with cyclic patterns. However, many cases remain unclear.

Multiple formal models can equivalently define functions that map infinite strings to other infinite strings, including MSO-transducers, streaming transducers, and certain two-way transducers. However, even when restricted to single passes through the input, some functions in these models can still be undecidable by Turing machines with infinite input, despite being defined by finite-state machines. To address this issue, a new decision-making approach is proposed for determining whether a specific function is computable and, if so, creating a corresponding Turing machine. 

For functions that map over finite alphabets, both computability and a corresponding Turing machine can be determined by analyzing whether a specific two-way streaming transducer accepts only computable input strings; if it does, an equivalent Turing machine can also be constructed. Furthermore, this approach allows for resolving one of the original issues related to deciding the convertibility of pushdown automata, which involves determining whether a specific class of context-free languages is equal to a specific class of regular tree languages.

Researchers have analyzed collision data with an integrated luminosity of 3 inverse femtobarns, and through amplitude analysis of specific two-body decay events, have discovered that the $B^0$ decay to a pair of $K^*$ mesons exhibits a higher fraction of longitudinal polarization than the $B^0_s$ decay to the same mesons. Furthermore, this difference in longitudinal polarization allows for a more precise measurement of the branching fraction of the $B^0$ decay to a pair of $K^*$ mesons.

A machine learning technique known as reservoir computing generates a model that mimics complex systems and accurately predicts their future behavior. When applied to a scenario with multiple coexisting patterns of behavior, the method demonstrates its ability to effectively predict previously unseen patterns of behavior on both numerical and real-world data sets.

A new bias-corrected estimator has been created for the mean absolute deviation of a median regression model, addressing a notable limitation of previous research in this area.  Establishing and verifying the properties of this estimator requires a critical examination of its asymptotic behavior.  Key findings include: (1) the estimator exhibits desirable properties such as zero bias under specific conditions, (2) its asymptotic behavior conforms to standard regression estimates, and (3) conditions can be relaxed through alternative definitions of consistency.  Building on existing research, a new bias-corrected estimator for median regression models has been introduced and its asymptotic properties verified.  Relating the study to prior research, a novel result is the creation of an asymptotically normal and efficient estimator for the mean absolute deviation, a significant advancement over previous work.

To address scalability issues with Eulerian methods for finding optimal controllers under constraints and worst-case disturbances in variational Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs formulations, we've developed a second-order successive sweep algorithm for calculating the reachable state space. This approach, which assumes a continuous and smooth Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equation, enables us to determine the states that can be reached within a given time frame under worst-case conditions and state feedback control.

Multi-Layer Perceptrons are particularly effective at generating accurate
low-dimensional representations of data, such as images, shapes and light
fields. Despite advancements using periodic activations or hierarchical
representations, a common issue persists - models are ineffective at transferring
their learned representations to new tasks or domains. To address this, we
propose a novel type of periodic activation function, one that adapts to its
input by modulating its periodic components. When integrated into a MLN, this
activation enhances the quality of its embeddings, while also facilitating
transfer learning. We demonstrate the efficacy of our periodic activation
by achieving exceptional results on challenging benchmark tests, including: (1)
extending the scope of learning to new viewpoints with the Devil in the
details benchmark, (2) efficiently using fewer parameters to represent new
categories with the mini-ImageNet benchmark, (3) accurately predicting
multiple future frames in the physics-based Light Field benchmark tests.
Furthermore, we show that our activation's adaptability enables it to
efficiently learn local features, while minimizing the need for global
representations.

The underlying mechanisms of the ventral temporal cortex's animacy organization remain contentious, suggesting that animacy exists along a spectrum rather than a binary divide. Recent evidence suggests this continuum is influenced by the degree of presence or absence of distinct animal features or by how entities are perceived as social agents. In this study, a stimulus set with independent factors of visual categorizability and agency perception in animals was used to test these hypotheses through both computational neural networks and behavioral experiments. Utilizing functional magnetic resonance imaging, our findings showed that visual categorizability and agency perception separately explained independent components of the animacy spectrum in VTC. When combined, they fully captured the continuum, and our data indicated distinct posterior regions associated with each. The results of this study demonstrate the complex nature of the animacy spectrum in VTC, revealing multiple governing principles such as social agency that shape our understanding of this phenomenon.

The study proves the nonexistence of Landau-Siegel zeros or confirms quantum unique ergodicity for GL_2 Hecke-Maass newforms at a calculable pace, supported by the broader conclusion that Dirichlet L-function zeros exert a force pushing zeros from all other automorphic L-functions off the s=1 axis.

We have adapted the quantum relational Hoare logic originally proposed in (Unruh, POPL 2019) to incorporate "expectations" into preconditions and postconditions, thereby enabling the quantification of pre-/postconditions that reflect the relationship between programs' inputs and outputs when comparing pairs of programs.

A significant phenomenon is observed in the early stages of epidemics worldwide, where a small number of high infectivity cases abruptly cause a sudden spike in reported daily infections. To understand and account for this notable effect, the term "super-spreader event" is commonly used. In mathematical modeling, incorporating such events is crucial to accurately predicting epidemic progression and developing effective control strategies. This article presents a novel approach to integrating super-spreader events into the standard SIR model, successfully simulating the rapid increase in daily infection rates commonly seen in early epidemic data. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that traditional SIR model-based predictions significantly overestimate the number of daily infections, highlighting the critical importance of incorporating super-spreader events in epidemiological modeling.

Let's consider a complex topological vector space, denoted as X, along with the collection L(X) of continuous linear operators that act on X. This paper seeks to expand the concept of codiskcyclicity, initially developed for a solitary operator within L(X), to a broader context of operator sets defined as $\Gamma\subset L(X).$ Some key results regarding codiskcyclic collections of operators are proven, accompanied by a codiskcyclicity criterion. Furthermore, we demonstrate its practical utility by investigating the codiskcyclicity of C_0-semigroups comprised of operators.

The paper addresses the problem of bias in vector magnetic field maps, particularly in estimating the component perpendicular to the line-of-sight, Bperp. This issue was identified by comparing observations with a model, CHIAR, and synthetic data from the SDO/HMI, and found to be present in multiple data sets. The source of the bias, found to be 57 Mxes, was shown to vary with solar activity and was different for local and global areas. The reason for this bias is not yet determined, but it may originate from an error in the inversion code, or an inherent limitation of the data and model used. Further investigation is advised to determine the cause and any necessary adjustments to the code.

A comprehensive study has been conducted to measure the radii of 6097 young star clusters in 31 galaxies from the LEGUS survey. The custom analysis method enabled the determination of radii for clusters at the edge of detected images. Typically, the measured radii ranged from 2-10 pixels, equivalent to 1-10 pc, with a median of approximately 3.3 pc. The calculated radii demonstrated a clear dependence on cluster brightness, with a median ratio of about 4.3, indicating that more luminous clusters tend to have larger radii. The relationship between cluster light and radius was found to be a linear function, with some curvature considered. The study found that the mass-light ratio of young star clusters, estimated as a linear function of mass, followed a universal form across the examined galaxies. Nevertheless, the ratio varied by 0.5-1.0 dex when comparing the most massive clusters in different galaxies. The analysis revealed little scatter in the M/L ratios of individual clusters, with a median of about 0.28, or a standard deviation of 0.073 in log space. The studied clusters displayed little or no offset in their M/L ratios when compared to the M/L ratios of the host galaxies' integrated light, except for a few galaxies requiring further exploration. The analysis also uncovered a relation between the light distribution of clusters and their mass, with more massive clusters following a exponential profile more frequently.

We present a novel, direct method for calculating the decay width of hadrons
decaying to two photons, often requiring an indirect estimation via off-shell
form factors. The new method offers an uncomplicated way to study volume effects.
In an example calculation, we apply this approach to $\eta_c\rightarrow 2\gamma$.
Using lattice ensembles with three $N_f=2$ configurations at different lattice
spacings, we derive the final decay width $\Gamma_{\eta_c\gamma\gamma}=6.57(15)_{\textrm{stat}}(8)_{\textrm{syst}}$ keV,
considering systematics in the charm quark mass. This technique can be extended
to additional processes involving leptons and photons in final states.

A sign problem encountered in Monte Carlo simulations beyond half-filling can be mitigated by transforming the integration path. However, this transformation introduces an additional computational cost associated with the Jacobian determinant in the Boltzmann weight, posing a significant barrier for large-scale simulations. Our proposed architecture, based on a novel application of complex-valued affine coupling layers in neural networks, efficiently circumvents this challenge by achieving linear scaling of the determinant cost. As a result, this method allows us to tackle intractably large systems plagued by a severe sign problem.

This paper examines the relationship between integers that are y-friable (or y-smooth) and the Dickman function. By assuming the Riemann Hypothesis (RH), we had a previous estimate of the count of y-friable integers up to x in terms of the Dickman function but it was limited to integers y greater than or equal to $(\log x)^2$. Our refinement improves this to y greater than or equal to $1.45677\log x$ after establishing that this gap lessens as x grows larger under the condition of RH. We also derive an analogous result for x-friable integers without any constraints on the relationship between x and y. 

Furthermore, we discuss the implications of our findings on the estimation of the count of y-friable integers among the first x integers. We also explore connections with previous works by Hildebrand and Saias and establish the exact upper bounds for the density of y-friable integers among all integers, incorporating both dense and sparse sets. 

In addition, we suggest and analyze several open questions related to our research.

Given any non-erasing free monoid morphism σ and subshift X, its image subshift Y under σ and the associated complexity functions p_X and p_Y exhibit the following relationship: there exist constants c, d, and C, where p_X scales by a factor of at least c times d, while scaling at most C, in the sufficiently large integers n in N. If σ is recognizable and letter-to-letter, then p_Y and p_X grow at similar rates, whereas if σ isn't letter-to-letter, there are instances where p_X isn't proportional to p_Y. As a result, topological entropy h_X isn't necessarily preserved when applying σ to X, indicating that defining topological entropy for free group currents isn't feasible. Nevertheless, if σ is a free monoid morphism that breaks down a free group basis into more independent generators, then the resulting topological entropies of the associated subshifts will be r times the original value, where r represents the number of new generators obtained.

By leveraging previously acquired skills and adapting them to unfamiliar tasks without explicit guidance, humans demonstrate impressive cross-task capabilities.
This study aims to enhance the cross-task generalization ability of massive language models in unsupervised settings, with a focus on models like T0 and FLAN.
We introduce a novel, unsupervised retrieval-augmentation method known as ReCross, which employs unlabeled samples to selectively draw from existing data, fine-tune the model for better performance.
The proposed method seamlessly integrates both high-efficiency dense retrieval and a more effective pair-wise re-ranking process to produce outstanding results, surpassing non-retrieval methods and alternative baselines in our experiments.

This research introduces the m-arcsinh Kernel ('m-ar-K') Fast Independent Component Analysis ('FastICA') approach ('m-ar-K-FastICA') for feature extraction in machine learning. By combining kernel-based dimensionality reduction with ICA, m-ar-K-FastICA offers a more effective method for extracting features from noisy data sets. Our proposed approach simplifies the kernel-based ICA process by utilizing a quadratic formula and bypasses the need for deriving the inverse kernel, thereby enhancing computational efficiency. Furthermore, the RStudio-friendly'm-ar-K-FastICA' R package is presented, demonstrating the algorithm's computational speed and accuracy in handling real-time data streams and large datasets, including those with categorical features and a large number of redundant features. Comparative evaluations with the classic FastICA algorithm and Minimum Barrier Method ('MBRICA') have validated the performance enhancements offered by the proposed approach.

This work offers an overview of requirements engineering in the gaming sector.
Existing research studies on this topic have been comprehensively examined.
Key characteristics of the gaming industry were identified and their connections to broader market dynamics discussed.
In addition, several potential areas for further research within this field were briefly highlighted.

Optimizing hyperparameters in the private version of the stochastic gradient descent algorithm is a critical issue due to limited access to private datasets for hyperparameter tuning. The development of algorithms that efficiently find optimal hyperparameters for a favorable balance between privacy and performance within a predetermined search space is, therefore, crucial. In this paper, a generalized framework is established to determine an optimal balance between privacy and performance, and three cost-effective algorithms are systematically examined within this framework: evolutionary optimization, Bayesian methods, and reinforcement learning. The results of our experiments, conducted using MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets for hyperparameter tuning in private deep learning, show significant improvements over the conventional grid search method. The paper addresses existing challenges and potential research directions in the field, and provides an open-source code for hyperparameter tuning in private deep learning.

For a Coxeter system denoted by (W,S), we develop the concept of a boolean complex consisting of involutions within W, mirroring Ragnarsson and Tenner's previous work. By applying discrete Morse theory, we identify the homotopy type of this boolean complex for a significant subset of Coxeter groups, including finite groups, revealing that its homotopy type is equivalent to that of a collection of spheres with dimension |S|-1. Moreover, we derive straightforward, recursive formulas to compute the number of spheres within this collection.

The Euclid satellite, set to launch in 2022, will significantly influence future cosmological research with its Visible and Near Infrared Spectrometer and Photometer instruments. The authors of this study analyzed how correlated readout noise affects in-flight measurements for the NISP detectors and proposed an efficient method for noise reduction. Through laboratory and laboratory-to-sky projections, they compared proposed and current flux measurement estimators, ultimately demonstrating that neglecting noise correlation can lead to inaccurate measurements and biased color measurements. The authors conclude that accounting for noise correlation is crucial and advocate for its consideration in the reevaluation of NISP's science cases.

We applied an advanced statistical approach to examine the composition of 34,410 stars in the Milky Way disk using a vast dataset from the APOGEE-2. The study involved using a two-component model to break down elemental patterns into supernovae types and then comparing observed values to predicted values. The comparison yielded small discrepancies of up to 0.1 dex in some cases. The study revealed relationships between elements including a group sharing similar variations and distinct groups of elements with different behaviors. It also shed light on stars that the model struggled to accurately account for, likely indicating physical variations and small errors in measurements. The study enabled a controlled comparison of different star populations based on factors such as metal content. The findings revealed similar elemental patterns in outer regions of the galaxy, variations in satellite galaxies and star clusters like omega Centauri, and differences in abundance of elements in outer regions compared to inner regions. The study paves the way for a deeper understanding of the formation and chemical evolution of the galaxy.

The COVID-19 pandemic spread globally in early 2020 and caused severe consequences in China, also exacerbating public health anxiety fueled by rampant online rumors. To address this pressing issue, we examined the dynamics of rumor propagation and proposed a method to measure the impact of a rumor by tracking the speed of its new adopters. Utilizing search frequency as a proxy for this metric, we identified the peak and attenuation coefficients which conform to an exponential distribution. Subsequently, we developed and evaluated machine learning models, discovering that decision trees effectively forecast the peak coefficient and linear regression accurately predicts the attenuation coefficient. Our analysis indicated that certain precursor characteristics are crucial for predicting a rumor's peak influence, whereas location and entity information have a less significant impact on the attenuation coefficient. The study's findings were validated through the evaluation of features and the selection of models. Furthermore, we explored the anxiety-causing potential of a rumor by analyzing its effect on microblog user anxiety in China during the COVID-19 pandemic.

A novel approach to measuring the distance to galaxies has been discovered by examining extragalactic planetary nebulae, specifically due to their nearly universal brightness pattern. Determining the precise distances to galaxies through planetary nebulae analysis depends on collecting comprehensive data sets, and the observed frequency of these nebulae directly correlates with the galaxies' overall mass. Therefore, researchers must either utilize wide-field observations or focus on the central areas of galaxies. By focusing on the central areas, a comprehensive study has been conducted of the planetary nebulae residing within early-type galaxies located within the Fornax cluster using spectroscopic observations taken from the VLT/MUSE data collection from the Fornax3D survey. By distinguishing nebular emissions from stellar continuum, a comprehensive database of planetary nebulae was compiled and their host galaxies' light variations accounted for, resulting in the detection of over 8000 distinct planetary nebulae. By comparing the observed frequencies of planetary nebulae to the expected masses of galaxies, a comprehensive database was created allowing for the estimation of galaxy masses and distances. This approach yielded reliable estimates for 12 galaxies, with a margin of error of under 0.03 in logarithmic units, providing a significant improvement to previous measurements made by the Hubble Space Telescope.

Every aspect of life, from personal routines to the workings of major organizations, is governed by time-based schedules. Despite this widespread pattern, conventional programing languages and frameworks often ignore temporal relationships in data, forcing developers to use workarounds to incorporate timing information. This interconnection between periodic data and time-based processing is so fundamental that it deserves a built-in concept similar to that of immutable objects or functions. This concept, when integrated into a programming language, would enable the compiler to optimize time-based processing efficiently. We have developed LifeStream, a high-performance stream processing engine designed to work in conjunction with a programming language that incorporates periodic data types natively. LifeStream uses a hybrid approach, combining low-level system programming with higher-level language constructs to create a stream processor that can operate directly on raw network packets. LifeStream achieves great performance by utilizing CPU instructions tailored to process packets efficiently and a runtime system that prevents unnecessary data copying. We have evaluated LifeStream's capability to process real-time data streams in conjunction with a programming language on a set of application benchmarks, and our results indicate that it outperforms specialized stream processors by a factor of ten to a hundred in terms of processing throughput.

This research paper confirms that certain types of curves, specifically those in higher dimensional space, do not fit the classification of Bertrand curves except in two-dimensional Euclidean space. A new category, called the timelike (1,3)-Bertrand curve, is defined to fill this gap and its characteristics are identified for curves in a four-dimensional Euclidean space.

The choice of loss function for a neural network is widely regarded as a key decision with far-reaching implications, given the numerous loss functions developed to date, making it crucial to carefully select one. Despite its significance, research on the topic often omits explicit justification for loss function selection. We contend that this lack of justification reflects an untested assumption prevalent within the deep learning community. In this research, we investigate how loss function impacts performance in a supervised classification context. Our findings reveal that certain, previously underappreciated loss functions, including the KL divergence, can yield superior outcomes compared to established methods, underscoring the need to view loss function choice as a parameter amenable to optimization, rather than a fixed constant.
A stabilizable boundary feedback controller is designed for the Navier-Stokes equations using a linear control scheme with an oblique boundary orientation.

This research aims to advance the understanding of thermomechanical behavior in polymer crystallization. Strain-induced crystallization plays a significant role in polymer mechanical and thermal properties and must be accounted for during production and final product application design. To effectively capture its mechanical and thermal impacts, a dual-scale approach is employed, separating crystalline and amorphous regions to model material mechanics and thermal dynamics. The model incorporates material degradation, temperature changes, and interphase interactions to predict phase changes, using the Herrington-Kennedy model for nucleation and Toda-Lai growth rate equations. Numerical testing validates the proposed model's accuracy and efficiency.

To analyze the impact of external magnetization on superconducting materials, we mathematically investigate the magnetic field's effect on a triplet $p$-wave superconductor in the presence of a uniaxial nematic disorder. Utilizing a method that accounts for both strong and moderate nematic disorder strengths, we calculate the magnetic susceptibility and find that the susceptibility follows a distinct nematic disorder-dependent characteristic. Specifically, in superconductors with strong nematic disorder, the magnetic susceptibility exhibits an opposing reaction to the applied field, displaying a maximum value at high nematic disorder strengths. This opposing reaction can occur at both extremely low and moderately low temperatures. Moreover, we establish that the nematic disorder has the potential to switch the superconductor's magnetic response from diamagnetic to paramagnetic, a phenomenon that could be detected through measurements of the magnetic susceptibility.

One significant issue in Imitation Learning (IL) is that obtaining perfect optimal demonstrations from a teacher is a challenging task due to the complexities involved, especially in robotics. Providing quality feedback is further constrained by the need to supply demonstrations for multiple state actions at once. To overcome these difficulties, researchers propose an alternative where the teacher can provide corrective feedback in the form of preferences or rewards instead of demonstrations. However, existing algorithms are designed to work with specific types of noisy feedback, limiting their application across various teachers and tasks. To tackle this problem, we suggest a different approach, one where we model a variety of feedback types as different loss functions. Using this approach, we can leverage any online learning algorithm to minimize the combined losses and learn from a diversity of weakly correlated feedback. Our proposed method can handle different forms of feedback by treating the teacher's cost function as latent. By applying a general corrective feedback meta-algorithm that unifies prior work, we can achieve similar regret bounds regardless of the type of feedback. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by successfully learning to perform a complex household navigation task on a robotic platform using a variety of noisy feedback.

Continuous phase modulation detection using conventional differential detection techniques is highly resistant to various channel disturbances, such as phase and Doppler shift. Its basic structure makes its implementation uncomplicated, involving the product of a received baseband signal and a time-reversed version of one symbol duration. Nevertheless, it experiences reduced signal-to-noise ratio compared to coherent detection methods. In this research, the performance of conventional differential detection is enhanced through increased delay periods. By accounting for $K$ symbol delays, the trellis structure and relevant branch and cumulative metrics are derived, resulting in an optimized criterion for $K$. This criterion is based on the minimum Euclidean distance between differential signals, ultimately facilitating the selection of ideal delay periods for popular CPM formats through simulated error rates verification.

New findings from 1D core-collapse simulations shed new light on the ultimate demise of massive stars, contradicting widely employed numerical models. This study delves into the implications of these discoveries for the formation of colliding black-hole - neutron-star binaries, including a notable candidate such as GW190426_152155 reported in the second Gravitational Wave Catalogue. Beyond restricting the progenitor's mass, the author examines how the new collapse physics affects the formation of neutron-star - black-hole binaries and mergers with no neutron star remnant. Utilizing a set of improved numerical models, a probability distribution of distinct Love star quotients is determined for each specific black-hole - neutron-star binary type, enhancing our understanding of these systems' formation and potential multi-messenger observations.

A previously reported finding from research on thermal quantum fields in spacetimes of varying metrics - specifically, the relationship between quantum capacity and vacuum compressibility in the spacetime - is further investigated. This research broadens the study to cover both high and low temperature conditions in four distinct metric configurations: de Sitter, Schwarzschild black holes, as well as their combinations in 2+1 and 1+2 dimensional scenarios. The relationship between the compressibility and capacity was found to be consistent across all temperatures and spacetime dimensions, providing support for a fundamental principle linking these two concepts. This principle is then applied to calculate the compressibility in scenarios where the capacity is known, such as for a massless scalar field in 4-dimensional spacetime. The findings also reveal that the ratio of the compressibility to capacitance is a universal constant, valued at approximately 0.382, across all temperatures and spacetime dimensions.

Current deep learning techniques used for removing rain from images have achieved notable success in processing artificially created rainy images.  Nonetheless, their effectiveness drastically drops when confronted with genuine rainy conditions, primarily because they often employ highly simplified models of rain which contrast with the complex real rain scenarios.  This study posits that rain simulation and image de-raining are mutually interconnected and hence seeks to simultaneously tackle both tasks via a disentangled image transformation approach.  This approach involves training two reverse image transformations - a rain simulation network that attempts to recreate a disentangled rainy image from a clear sky image, and an image de-raining network that attempts to extract a disentangled background image from a real rainy image.  The training of both transformations is synchronized, with the aim of producing a disentangled rainy image that when combined with the clear sky image yields the original rainy image.  This approach is efficient and enables the removal of real rain from images in addition to synthetic rain.  The code for this study is available at https://github.com/yinggran/Closing-the-loop.

A prominent paradigm in reward learning utilizes human feedback via comparative evaluations, but their broader adoption is hindered by the expense and labor intensity of these comparisons. To overcome this limitation, we propose grouping multiple comparisons together and allowing human labelers to mark sub-regions of a condensed state space representation, thereby efficiently leveraging human time. Through data visualization techniques, we create an interactive interface for users to label these regions, thereby effectively enhancing the learning agents' performance, even when human labeling time remains constant, across basic Mujoco tasks.

We discuss recent research findings regarding model companions in set theory within the context of ongoing debates in the philosophy of mathematics. Initially, we explore how the concept of model companions is affected by the signature, before specifically examining the dependence of model companions in set theory. Our analysis indicates that the most intrinsic model companions for set theory correspond to $H_{\kappa^+}$ theories, as the infinite cardinal $\kappa$ varies. Furthermore, we highlight that the Continuum problem has a singular solution of $2^{\aleph_0}=\aleph_2$, which aligns with some model companion of enriched set theory containing large cardinal axioms. This model-theoretic framework is justified by a maximality concept reminiscent of Hilbert's axiom of completeness.
This study establishes conditions and proof of existence for a modified Branson-Paneitz equation under Navier boundary conditions on a finite region of n-dimensional Euclidean space.

Evaluating a person's risk of drug abuse is crucial for both rehabilitation efforts and community safety. The theory behind this study suggests that a person's personality, specifically their extraversion and impulsivity traits, play a key role in their tendency to engage in harmful drug consumption behavior. Based on neuroticism's established link to maladaptive coping mechanisms and low conscientiousness's association with impulsive decisions, it's reasonable to assume these traits also contribute to increased drug consumption risk. Extraversion's potential link was less clear, so this study aimed to investigate it as well. Utilizing a sample of 1264 participants from the Human Functional Connectome Project, researchers employed statistical modeling to examine the relationship between the five factor model of personality and drug consumption behavior across various substances. Their findings confirmed the expected connections between neuroticism, conscientiousness, and drug consumption and further revealed a novel, negative correlation between extraversion and drug consumption.

Our proposed dataset, ATOMIC, is an exhaustive collection of everyday commonsense reasoning rules comprising nearly a million text-based descriptions.  This atlas of inferential knowledge, structured as conditional relationships (if X, then Y), stands out from other available datasets that are centered on categorization, by providing a framework that accounts for causality and effects, actions versus thoughts, and intentional versus unintentional actions.  We have developed nine categories of these relationships and demonstrated the efficacy of incorporating these patterns into models of artificial intelligence.  Our findings reveal that through generative training on ATOMIC, our models have gained a capacity for basic reasoning about events that are novel.  This is supported by test results showing that machine learning models incorporating these patterns achieve more accurate outcomes in relation to models operating in isolation as judged by both automated assessments and human feedback.

Portfolio optimization is a critical application in Finance, yet its computational intricacies compel financial institutions to rely on simplified methods, which do not account for market dynamics and lead to suboptimal investment choices when facing rare events. Contemporary quantum algorithms, specifically variance reduction HHL+VR and NISQ-friendly hybrid HHL, exhibit enhanced efficiency and robustness on Noisy Intermediate Scale Quantum devices, facilitating the optimization of portfolios with considerations for rare events. This research introduces a novel hybrid approach, NISQ-HHL VR, combining the benefits of HHL+VR and conventional backpropagation in a quantum-classical hybrid framework, enabling efficient and differentiable matrix inversion and enabling the optimization of portfolios with considerations for rare events on Noisy Quantum devices. Furthermore, this research showcases the efficacy of NISQ-HHL VR VR through the development of a prototype, with resultant performance outperforming classical methods on large-scale problems and demonstrating improved gradient descent stability on Noisy Quantum devices.

To enhance data efficiency of state-of-the-art end-to-end ASR models and enable them to handle a large amount of unpaired text data through multi-modal training, it's essential to address two challenges: synchronizing the sampling rates of speech and language features and ensuring that the learned representations from both encoders are consistent. This paper introduces a novel bidirectional attention mechanism that combines the learning of both the ASR and text encoders using a multi-modal learning method. This attention mechanism facilitates the exchange of sampling rates, effectively allowing the quality of transformed features to be measured in an alternative space. This leads to speech representations being enriched with more linguistic information, while the text representations are made more similar to speech, enabling ASR models to effectively leverage unpaired text data for pretraining. Experimental evaluations on the Librispeech corpus reveal a significant 6.15% reduction in word error rate when only paired data is used and up to 9.23% when additional unpaired text data is applied.

This analysis addresses the challenge of optimizing cross-sectional area through a specific point within a geometric form. To generalize this concept, the approach is expanded across multiple dimensions. Nonetheless, the optimal average cross-sectional volume cannot be achieved unless cross-sections pass through the centroid of the shape. Therefore, the focus is on stationary shapes with optimal average cross-section properties. A new formula is introduced for average cross-section calculations in any dimension, and the associated equation of stationary shapes is derived. Properties of stationary shapes are discussed through mathematical derivation, numerical modeling, and graphical visualization. Additionally, the distinct properties of stationary shapes in 2D, 3D, and 5D are explored and analyzed.

This paper investigates the long-term behavior of a randomly generated uniform parking distribution of size $n$, denoted as $\pi_n$. We establish that the first $k_n$ positions of $\pi_n$, $\pi_n(1)$ through $\pi_n(k_n)$, are asymptotically independent and identically distributed with a uniform probability distribution over the set $\{1, 2, \dots, n\}$ for two different distance metrics. When the number of initial positions $k_n$ grows at a rate slower than $\sqrt{n}$ for the total variation distance and slower than $n$ for the Kolmogorov distance, this asymptotic behavior is shown, thereby extending previous findings by Diaconis and Hicks. Furthermore, this work also derives rate bounds and statistical limit theorems for the sum or the maximum of the first $k_n$ parking locations. Our main approach to achieving these results is by utilizing conditioned random walk reformulations.

Measurements of superconducting nanowires, particularly NbN nanowires, indicate the presence of a critical voltage threshold for dc conduction below which coherent quantum phase slips dominate, potentially blocking conduction. The critical voltage of these nanowires is observed to be tunable using an adjacent gate electrode and varies significantly in response to applied voltage, aligning with expected results of quantum interference but exhibiting unanticipated periodic variations. The magnitude of these periodic variations far exceeds predictions based on capacitance alone and presents a discrepancy in understanding this phenomenon, especially after observing sudden period shifts during measurements. The conducted experiments were performed under controlled conditions to minimize influence from environmental factors and the variability of nanowire properties, allowing for a focused examination of the effects in question.

The discovery of T-dwarf GJ 229B in 1995 offered initial insight into its composition, yet a detailed analysis with current spectroscopic methods has been lacking for nearly three decades. Utilizing a sophisticated algorithm called APOLLO for combined analysis of high-resolution spectra and light curves, we have a fundamental understanding of GJ 229B's properties for the first time since its discovery. Our analysis of high-resolution spectra from the TRES and HIRES telescopes enabled the retrieval of a highly accurate atmospheric model, confirming previous findings that GJ 229B has a highly indeterminate rotation period. Combining our analysis with previous observations of light curves, we have determined a solution indicating the star has a mass similar to that of the central body it orbits, GJ 229, around 0.5 solar masses, with a highly eccentric orbit of 0.87 eccentricity and a temperature of approximately 1000 K. Our data also suggest the existence of a possible, as-yet-unobserved mini-planetary body with a mass greater than 0.01 Jupiter masses in a highly tilted, almost circular orbit around GJ 229B, offering a possible explanation for the star's unstable rotation period.

Our study offers an explanation of the structural properties of a thermal medium like quark-gluon plasma, using the framework of electron scattering via virtual photons on this medium. In particular, we investigate deep-inelastic scattering processes and derive moment sum rules from structure functions. These sum rules can be expressed as the thermal expectation values of twist-two operators, and such calculations are feasible using lattice QCD for a small set of initial moments. We demonstrate how lattice simulations can determine the minimum virtuality for a photon needed for Bjorken scaling to apply to structure functions. Additionally, we explain the parton model representation of the structure functions within the Bjorken limit and assess its coherence. In line with typical DIS on protons, a kinematic parameter $x$ here directly represents the momentum carried by the partons, with its value spanning from zero to infinity. If the partons' momenta are parametrized as $x T u$, with $u$ being the four-velocity of the fluid and $T$ the temperature in its rest frame, the distribution of quarks within the non-interacting quark plasma follows $x \log(1+e^{-x/T})$.

Our proposed approach tackles the challenge of novel view video prediction, taking input from multiple viewpoints. Unlike existing research that relies on narrow angle variations, our network can generate videos from significantly wider angles, up to 45 degrees, without the need for prior knowledge. By processing only RGB frames, we've developed a two-component representation, combining local and global features that enables novel view prediction. Our model achieves remarkable results on real-world datasets NTU-RGB+D and CMU Panoptic, surpassing the state-of-the-art in novel view video prediction, demonstrating significant gains in SSIM, PSNR, and FVD scores of 26.1%, 13.6%, and 60% respectively, without the use of prior views.

In this research, inter-orbital coupling was demonstrated using femtosecond laser writing, which enables orthogonal modes in a photonic lattice to couple with each other at different spatial locations. We characterized an asymmetric double-well structure, mapped its propagation dynamics and successfully created a device capable of spatial mode conversion anywhere within a photonic chip. Utilizing higher-order photonic mode phase structure, our experiment showed that a trimer configuration can serve as a $\pi$-phase beam splitter for multiplexing and other interference-based photonic applications.

The Ω-baryon, which contains sss quarks and has only been marginally detected in past experiments, has primarily been studied using theoretical methods so far. A study aims to explore this particle's properties utilizing a quark model with linear confining forces. Calculated resonance masses are presented for the ground and excited states of S, P, D, and F quark systems. A linear nature of the Regge trajectory, supported by calculated data and magnetic moments, has also been examined. This study compares its results to other approaches and available experimental evidence.

Airborne transmission risk in confined environments like buses is intricately affected by the interplay between turbulent airflow, respiration processes, coughing, and sneezing, as well as various ventilation methods, temperature-driven buoyancy effects, and surface deposition of aerosols. To better understand and quantify this complex dynamic, we used numerical models of unsteady airflow to analyze and visualize virus-laden aerosol transport. In comparing our detailed model to a widely accepted 'well mixed' model, notable discrepancies in the distribution of aerosol particles became evident, with implications for our understanding of the spread of airborne pathogens. Furthermore, the differences identified in our study are expected to be relevant to a broader range of enclosed settings beyond urban buses.

Building on cutting-edge experimental projects such as HIBEF at the XFEL, our calculations investigate the birefringent scattering of x-rays when interacting with two combined optical lasers, considering various possible outcomes. To aid in detecting quantum vacuum effects experimentally, our analysis focuses particularly on situations where x-ray photons show differences not just in polarization, but also in direction of propagation and potential energy changes.

This note outlines the algorithm devised by J. M. Eisenlohr and S. L. Farris to
systematically generate all fully transitive polyhedra in $d$-dimensional Euclidean space. Furthermore, this algorithm is employed to construct a novel polyhedron within three-dimensional Euclidean space.

Broadbent and Lord introduced the concept of unclonable encryption, a unique feature in an encryption scheme where an adversary can't produce two encrypted versions of the same original message from a given ciphertext. Our research expands upon this concept, focusing on several aspects:

  - Flexibility in Usage: We've identified a significant drawback in the previous unclonable encryption constructions by Broadbent and Lord, as they either only guarantee single-use security in the plain model or security in the random oracle model. Our research presents two novel constructions for both public-key and private-key settings that maintain security even after repeated use and are founded on minimal assumptions.

  - Understanding Cloning Capacity: We've investigated the one-time secure construction proposed by Broadbent and Lord, specifically aiming to determine if achieving a nearly optimal $0.5^n$ success probability for cloning is attainable. Our findings generalize the construction based on various forms of monogamy of entanglement and present attacks against specific schemes with cloning probabilities reaching as high as $0.75^n$.

  - Applications to Copy Protection: We've discovered that strong forms of unclonable encryption can lead to enhanced security, specifically copy-protection for unlearnable functions. Our research paves the way for potential new constructions meeting these requirements, thereby expanding the realm of copy-protection protocols protectable by their entanglement-based inspiration.

This study confirms that physical layer-based authentication is achievable in
Gaussian noise environments, with the caveat that an all-knowing adversary cannot be
beated. An examination of a model comprising encoder, decoder, and adversary was
carried out, with the latter possessing unlimited transmission capabilities and
unlimited access to the transmitted message. It was demonstrated that modifying an
existing communication protocol can enable secure transmission with negligible
efficiency loss, providing an increase in authenticator security of at least $2^r$
times, where $r$ is the number of secure bits. Furthermore, this technique does not
rely on specific characteristics of the communication protocol and can be applied to
any real-valued Gaussian noise environment. A secure transmission protocol with
negligible efficiency loss was proposed and shown to achieve $2^{1080}$ times
improvement in security level compared to standard 128-bit security level, assuming
$10^9$ transmitted bits. This approach may have practical implications for the
development of secure communication systems.

We utilized the full tight-binding model and random phase approximation to
explore flat-band plasmons in hole-doped twisted bilayer molybdenum disulfide.
Our calculations showed that lattice relaxation influences plasmon behavior.
When we considered intraband transitions, low-damped, flat plasmons emerged,
while accounting for interband transitions led to plasmon dispersion following
$\sqrt q$ law. The plasmon energies in these materials can be adjusted through
tweaking the twist angles and doping levels. For samples without lattice
relaxations, coexistence of low and high-energy plasmons occurs. Higher doping
levels however eliminate the quasi-flat plasmon. These observations imply that
two conditions must be satisfied: a flat band isolated from the other bands
and adequate doping level to witness the quasi-flat plasmon. The study offers
clues for exploring superconductivity mediated by plasmons in these materials.

This paper expresses the potential function $f$ associated with an almost conformal gradient Ricci soliton on a Sasakian manifold in terms of the scalar field $p$, determining when the potential function is constant, and establishing a link between $f$ and $\lambda$. We also establish a condition for a conformal Ricci soliton to be a gradient Ricci soliton, and provide a characterization of the soliton in terms of its contraction or expansion rate.

Both celestial bodies can experience mass loss due to the expansion of heated surrounding gas, created by magnetic interactions with the surrounding environment, or the flow of high-energy particles. This process forms a magnetized barrier that slows the loss of mass. The interaction between the magnetized barrier and the surrounding gas then generates characteristic signatures in the surrounding space. To study this phenomenon, researchers have developed multiple methods to analyze MHD shocks in various contexts. By comparing results from numerical simulations and theoretical models, similarities and differences can be identified in the patterns of energy generated by the process, as well as how they affect the surrounding gas. For example, the way energy is distributed across different wavelengths of light can provide clues about the nature of the magnetic field. Furthermore, the movement of gas can reveal information about the presence of rotating magnetic fields. Analyzing these phenomena can offer insights into the magnetic field structure of stars and planets.

The Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect involves a rise in Spin-Orbit Coupling near a strong spin-orbit material's interface with an adjacent layer. This phenomenon has been observed in various systems, such as graphene and ferromagnetic layers, and controlling Spin-Orbit Coupling is crucial for optimizing performance in SOPE-based devices. Our research involves investigating the electrical transport characteristics of Co/Bi multilayers to reveal the influence of Bi's crystallographic orientation on the anomalous Hall effect and the Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect. By combining Anomalous Hall Effect and Heavy Fermion-like behaviors analysis, our findings indicate that the presence of Bi layers contributes to both increased Spin-Orbit Coupling and carrier density.
