We examine the applicability and limitations of this approach to a broad category of self-similar diffusion processes, utilizing a general framework that is subsequently applied to recognized processes such as Laplace diffusion, nonlinear diffusion, and their variants.

A fundamental theory is developed to describe both linear and Kerr nonlinear interactions between the modes of dielectric optical resonators, with the framework being applicable across various geometries and modes. The general approach allows for a wide range of phenomena resulting from linear interactions, scattering, and Kerr nonlinearity, such as mode coupling and phase modulation, to be analyzed. The developed theory is specifically applied to a waveguide with a microresonator in close proximity, enabling the computation of mode coupling and phase modulation terms. Furthermore, a dimensionless equation is derived to describe the dynamics of two identical counterpropagating modes in a loop resonator and, under the condition of mode identity, it is proven that cross-phase modulation is precisely twice as strong as self-phase modulation.

This paper builds upon established connections between global asymptotic controllability, stabilizability, and control Lyapunov functions in control systems that allow unbounded controls, encompassing polynomial control systems. Our analysis specifically addresses unbounded open-loop controls and discontinuous feedback stabilizers, which may lead to trajectories exhibiting chattering behavior near the target. A central aspect of our findings is the demonstration of the equivalence between global asymptotic controllability, stabilizability, and control Lyapunov functions in these control systems or their impulsive system extensions.

A recent study proposes a novel deep learning approach that utilizes generative adversarial networks to generate highly detailed turbulent velocity patterns from limited-resolution data across a range of Reynolds numbers. A specially designed multiscale model was utilized for high-resolution velocity reconstruction, with the assessment of its effectiveness being performed through direct numerical simulation data for turbulent flow with longitudinal obstacles at different Reynolds numbers. The evaluation showed that this deep learning framework accurately replicates high-resolution velocity patterns and statistical measures from two low-resolution data sets. Furthermore, it was observed that this model successfully recreates turbulent velocity patterns at Reynolds numbers that it was not originally trained on.

The paper addresses misconceptions surrounding Jefimenko's equations, which are derived from Maxwell's equations, for a specific charge and current configuration obeying the continuity equation. It subsequently derives a non-radiative condition across inertial frames, consistent with the stability requirements of an atom, and establishes that this condition is analogous to certain relationships between charge, current, and the wave equations. The paper then demonstrates that these relationships lead to quantised electromagnetic field energy displaying the characteristics of the Balmer series.

Machine learning models, particularly those with open-world settings, encounter unknown categories that weren't accounted for during training. The presence of unknown categories significantly degrades performance when they're misclassified as known ones. A common issue with existing classification techniques is their inability to accurately model uncertainty when encountering novel categories. A novel uncertainty model has been developed that generalizes to any training setup, including closed-world scenarios. It employs an innovative energy-based function to model uncertainty, which is trained alongside the classification model through contrastive loss. The new uncertainty model outperforms several benchmarks in various evaluation metrics, demonstrating its effectiveness across multiple datasets and classification settings.

Despite notable breakthroughs in reinforcement learning, numerous significant hurdles remain when applying it to dynamic and ever-changing problems common in critical domains, including robotics and complex gameplay. Reinforcement learning models generally struggle to generalize effectively when faced with new tasks beyond their training data. In response to this challenge, the field is seeing an increased focus on continual learning methods, and to support this research, we present L2Explorer, a comprehensive evaluation environment designed to assess lifelong reinforcement learning performance. This complex 3D platform is characterized by multiple continuous state dimensions and a complex reward structure. To evaluate the efficacy of RLSI methods, we developed multiple challenging evaluation protocols. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of multiple state-of-the-art RLSI algorithms in L2Explorer. Notably, L2Explorer builds upon the foundation established by the procedurally generated exploration environments, MetaWorld, MetaGraphs, and MetaMaze, by incorporating multiple changes, including increased state dimensions, a non-stationary reward structure, and multiple continuous goal states.

Understanding business processes relies on process discovery methods, analyzing data trails to reveal underlying processes. Our approach develops a monitoring technique that uses data trails to identify processes by matching process executions against a reference model, and discovers processes by building a model from data trails without prior executions to compare against. This technique is efficient due to its focus on a single process instance and limited data trail set. Our approach enhances process visibility through analysis of execution history, providing insights into process behavior and detecting deviations from expected patterns.

In one-dimensional quasiperiodic structures, certain types of wave propagation exhibit a sudden shift from localization to non-localization. Our theory and experimental results indicate that in one-dimensional photonic quasicrystals, light localization can transition back to non-localization at higher quasiperiodic modulation strengths for some states, representing an unusual phenomenon. Additionally, this occurrence can be understood through a mathematical model that represents dimerized interactions over extended distances.

Liger, a next-generation infrared device at the W. M. Keck Observatory, will be paired with the Keck All-sky Precision Adaptive-optics system to optimize performance. By covering the wavelength range from 0.81 micrometers to 2.45 micrometers, Liger combines multiple observing modes, offering various spatial scales and fields of view. However, Liger's data complexity necessitates a customized data processing system to refine its output in real-time, making it compatible with science-oriented data presentation tools. This processing system, called the Data Reduction System, will be responsible for delivering refined data to astronomers and uploading it to the Keck Observatory Archive. We have established a prototype of this data processing system and defined the communication interface with the relevant software systems at the observatory.

Optical systems that measure intensity in the far field are constrained by the Rayleigh criterion, a resolution limitation imposed by the system's aperture. Research has shown that using spatial mode demultiplexing (SPADE) allows for maximum collection of field information, thereby overcoming the Rayleigh criterion in the near field. However, the minimum SPADE resolution is bounded by the higher of the two values determined by the Rayleigh criterion and the system's spherical aberration. Investigating a bi-photon system where SPADE is performed on two photons that originate from the same source, we find that the latter value dominates the minimum SPADE resolution. Notably, this limit can be broken when the photons' spatial modes exhibit a high amount of overlap. Furthermore, our research demonstrates that, under optimal conditions, the minimum SPADE resolution can achieve values below the diffraction limit. The findings can be applied to any optical system that measures intensity in the far field, ultimately enabling the improvement of its resolving power.
This note provides an introduction to the interplay between Hodge-theoretic and geometric approaches to compactifying moduli spaces of algebraic varieties.

In the study of population dynamics, identifying early warning indicators for sudden population changes and the mechanisms that lead to regime shifts is highly beneficial. This paper focuses on a model consisting of a two-level ecosystem where two species of predators, competing for a common prey in an enclosed space, exhibit complex population patterns. Due to the presence of a critical point where the population cycles change from stable to unstable, the model requires further examination. Although the model displays chaotic behavior in the unstable regime, specific 'ghost' periodic patterns can be observed. The research reveals that specific short-term changes in the prey population can serve as early indicators for the population entering a regime shift and ultimately failing to recover from a transient period. The model also demonstrates that in the stable regime, the population exhibits a stable, oscillatory pattern in line with the principles of Hassel-Yoshida dynamics. Furthermore, the findings indicate that in the unstable regime, the population's two-timescale behavior leads to frequency-locking and the generation of stable, long-period patterns. The research presented in this paper applies to a specific model but raises key questions that can be explored across a broader range of two-timescale predator-prey models.

Determining how star formation rates are controlled still poses a significant challenge for researchers in the field. One notable pattern is the negative correlation between the rate of star formation and the mass of galaxies, which only breaks down for the most massive galaxies. Building on previous findings, our analysis reveals that the rate of star formation in bulge-dominated galaxies falls below expected rates, consistent with the idea that the bulge's formation is linked to reduced star formation. Furthermore, rather than a distinct population, massive low-sensitivity galaxies can be modeled as bulge-dominated galaxies with a history of rapid star formation. By focusing solely on the disk components of these galaxies, we observe their star formation rates align with the -SFR relation. Therefore, the divergence from this relation in massive galaxies can be attributed to the presence of a bulge, which suggests that its formation may indicate a shift in the galaxy's star formation controls.

This paper conducts a sentiment analysis across languages, examining the
emotional content of news articles using both few-shot and zero-shot learning
techniques. The primary objective is to categorize Croatian news articles as
expressing positive, negative, or neutral sentiment, employing a model that
draws upon training data from Hungarian sources. In the few-shot learning phase,
the model utilizes a limited number of Croatian examples to inform its decisions,
while in the zero-shot learning phase, it relies solely on the training data from
Hungarian, applying this knowledge to interpret the Croatian data through translation
tables. The best model for each phase, one based on multilingual BERT and another
on LSTM, is then selected to make the sentiment classifications. The results show
that the BERT-based model achieves more accurate ratings in the few-shot learning
phase and the LSTM model in the zero-shot learning phase.

Recently, cache coherence protocols based on self-invalidation and self-downgrade have gained more recognition due to their minimalistic design, potential for increased performance efficiency, and reduced energy consumption. However, potential flaws in this approach need further exploration. This paper formally analyzes the fences of shared memory elements in SISD-like programs using self-invalidation and self-downgrade coherence protocols. Our model assesses the memory safety of these programs by validating the fence orders derived from the protocol's specifications. Our analysis develops a memory safety formula derived from the protocol's self-invalidation and self-downgrade properties. This formula serves as the foundation for validating the memory safety of program configurations consisting of coherence protocols based on self-invalidation and self-downgrade. To demonstrate the practical applications of this framework, we conduct a comprehensive validation of a set of program examples with a prototype cache simulator. The results show that our framework is capable of accurately identifying both correct and faulty program configurations. Furthermore, our framework can provide specific error reports that provide valuable insights for optimizing the performance of programs with suboptimal error patterns. These optimizations have the potential to convert programs with error patterns into those with correct memory safety, solely by inserting additional memory fence instructions.

Freiman's 3k-4 theorem generally posits that if subsets A and B, of size k and comprised of integers, share a sumset with a size near 2k, then A and B exhibit considerable similarity to arithmetic progressions. In this paper, we aim to enhance this by limiting the number of possible summands available from subset B. It's shown that if subsets A and B, of size k, meet the criterion that for every four-element subset of B, the sumset A plus that subset doesn't exceed 2k, it follows that A and B exhibit considerable similarity to arithmetic progressions.

Consider a fractional Brownian motion $B^{H}$ in $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ with Hurst index $H$ in the interval $(0,1)$. Let $f$ be a Borel function from $[0,1]$ to $\mathbb{R}^{d}$, and $A$ a Borel subset of $[0,1]$. Conditions will be established under which the image $(B^{H}+f)(A)$ has a positive Lebesgue measure or a non-empty interior. This is achieved through investigating properties of the occupation measure's density for $(B^{H}+f)$, particularly proving that if the parabolic Hausdorff dimension of $f$ exceeds $Hd$, then its density function is square-integrable, or if $A$'s Hausdorff dimension surpasses $Hd$, then its density function admits a continuous version, thus providing a result already mentioned.

Using Dirac's time-dependent variational principle, we establish a simple H\'enon-Heiles model based on semicircular geometry, focusing on a two-body trial wavefunction with separated harmonic oscillators. Applying Jackiw-Kerman methodology, we calculate the energy values and find that they transition from stable to chaotic levels within the H\'enon-Heiles model, mimicking the original scenario.

X-ray images contain subtle characteristics with predictive information about patients who are likely to experience severe COVID-19 symptoms.  If accurately identified, this could help prioritize high-risk patients for full lung imaging and subsequent treatment in ICU.  Although current automated COVID-19 detection systems effectively identify infected patients, they do not differentiate between patients who will require ICU admission and those who will not.  Our research proposes a novel approach to detecting features in X-ray images that indicate patients may need lung imaging, even if their oxygen levels are normal.  To improve model accuracy, we increased the size of the training dataset, incorporated data from multiple hospitals, and designed a model that resists overfitting.  Our experiment demonstrated that, yes, it is possible to identify relevant image characteristics that suggest patients may need lung imaging based on X-ray images.

The classical universal bundle functor W mapping from the category of simplicial groups in C to the category of simplicial sets in C lifts to a monadic structure on the category of simplicial groups in C, and this extension holds for simplicial algebras defined by any Lawvere theory that includes group theory.

This paper delves into the source of high false positive rates in Visual Relationship Detection (VRD). During training, we discovered that the relationship proposal distribution is skewed, with the majority of incorrect relationships being easily identified due to poor object detection. As a result, low-frequency difficult proposals struggle to contribute effectively. Our proposed framework, Spatially-Aware Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (SABRA), addresses this imbalance and reduces false positives. In order to counter the issue of proposal sampling being dominated by easy negatives, we implemented a balanced sampling approach in the training phase. Additionally, we incorporated a difficult proposal mask and sampling strategy in the inference phase. Our method achieves superior performance and reduced false positives on the Visual Relationship Detection task, as evidenced by enhanced precision and balanced proposal distributions in our experiments on the Visual Genome and Visual Relationship Detection datasets.

This study offers a supervised action recognition solution that's effective even in the absence of light. We've obtained promising results by testing our approach on the ARID dataset, a significantly smaller and darker collection of video data. Notably, previous action recognition methods in the field typically rely on well-lit datasets such as Kinetics and HMDB51. Our results indicate that our technique achieves remarkable accuracy despite being trained on a much reduced and poorly lit dataset of video sequences. We've experimented with multiple training and prediction methods including cross-domain techniques, as well as introducing an efficient yet straightforward approach for frame selection. Our research demonstrates that action recognition is feasible with minimal lighting through predicting actions in a completely dark environment shot from a security camera.

This report outlines the development of a novel Content Addressable Parallel Processor, built with a Field Programmable Gate Array. Although content-addressable memories have been successfully implemented on FPGAs, our design uniquely captures Caxton C. Foster's pioneering ideas on parallel processing, incorporating the concepts of simultaneous parallel writes and the merging of output values – features commonly omitted in typical CAM applications like network routing. The resulting system allows a host computer to interface with the CAPP over USB/UART using a simple serial communication protocol, which has been effectively demonstrated with a Python-based driver.

We've performed an in-depth analysis of three galaxy cores at $\rm z=2.91$ within a massive galaxy group, yielding high-resolution infrared and submillimeter data. Our study reveals that the galaxies exhibit extremely compact, actively star-forming cores at the centers of massive, irregularly shaped disk systems. A3-factor analysis allowed us to deconstruct the galaxy's mass distribution and dynamics. We discovered that the massive disk systems are composed of freely moving, nearly circular orbiting matter, whereas the galaxy cores show signs of internal stress and potential black hole feedback. We constructed a theoretical model to explain the formation of the compact, actively star-forming cores, suggesting they developed from the accumulation of gas drawn from the disk by tidal forces. This process resulted in the irregular disk shape and slowed star formation elsewhere in the disk. We also discovered a previously overlooked galaxy, APM 0944-00, that exhibits similar features and may provide a more developed stage of this process.

We re-examine and revise the predictions of the Universal Texture Zero (UTZ) flavour model as initially presented in the study arXiv:1710.01741. The revision is made with reference to more accurate experimental restrictions and refined numerical analysis methods. Specifically, our team developed an in-house Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithm to extensively evaluate the viable parameter range of the UTZ model, encompassing primary and secondary contributions in its effective operator expansion. Furthermore, we obtained for the first time precise UTZ predictions for previously underdetermined CP-violating phases of lepton interactions, and related neutrino mass characterizing ratio observables, that could be probed via oscillations, beta decay, and cosmological processes. Consequently, our revised analysis significantly surpasses the initial analysis and confirms that the UTZ theory remains a coherent and compelling flavour theory. The findings also highlight the capability of robust MCMC analyses in evaluating multi-dimensional global fits of flavour models, making them invaluable tools for the theoretical flavour physics community.

We examine a specific nonlinear elliptic equation in R^N, where N is 5 or greater. No studies on the periodicity of its solutions have been done previously, so we explore related issues by making some key assumptions about a given function, Q(y), which is periodic and has a minimum value at zero. We demonstrate that numerous "bubbling solutions" for this equation exist and can be classified in a specific way when these conditions are met, resulting in some of these solutions maintaining the same symmetry as Q(y). Additionally, we find that "bubbling solutions" will not exist under alternative circumstances when Q(y)'s local minimum is zero, specifically in instances when it does not equal zero.

Current cutting-edge neural code models excel at generating individual code segments but often struggle with complex tasks, like entire function code production. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel approach that leverages static code analysis for weak supervision. Our neuro-symbolic method allows a deep neural network to contribute semantic information about a partially complete code snippet's intended variables and control flow. In return, an abstract syntax tree parser utilizes this information to guide the generation of the missing code segments with properly aligned variables and control flow. Empirical evaluations using the Python dataset reveal that our approach significantly outperforms state-of-the-art models in code generation tasks.

Recently discovered solar observations from the Nicaraguan GPS network and Mexican GPS network, operating since 2001 and providing real-time data, led to the detection of a significant increase of proton flux on November 7, 2004. This detection, initially reported by Hernández-Altamirano et al. in 2005, remained unverified until the recovery of raw data from the Nicaraguan GPS receivers. Analyzing the data from two Nicaraguan sites, using newly developed proton flux correction tools for scintillator detectors and reevaluating the original findings, our results confidently confirm the detection of the November 7, 2004 event, showing a proton flux peak around 17:05 UTC, with a duration of approximately one hour. This event is unique as it was observed from two distinct locations on the Earth's surface and offers valuable insights into the neutron decay proton spectrum, indicating a flux density of $(5.8\pm1.1) \times 10^{9}$ protons/m$^2$/s/MeV, over the energy range 10-190 MeV.

We have determined the dispersion relations for relativistic fluid modes in various configurations - scalar, vector, and tensor - and found the differences between their behavior in divergence-based and relaxation-time-approximation models. Our comparison also shows correspondence with first-order causal theories and highlights how a specific divergence-based model can predict damped tensor waves. This aligns with kinetic theory's results. It's interesting that both hydrodynamic and holographic fluids display similar properties. These findings reinforce the feasibility of using hydrodynamics to analyze the interaction between gravitational waves and fluids.

Real-time anomaly detection in continuous data streams presents difficulties for conventional and advanced methods due to shifting concepts and ongoing learning requirements. Existing approaches, such as using hash functions or nearest neighbors with fixed memory, can struggle to accommodate frequent fluctuations, remove smooth outliers, and adapt to deep neural network architectures. We introduce a new technique for continuous real-time anomaly detection based on quantum measurements, which can process infinite data streams at constant $O(1)$ update complexity and effectively estimate changing densities through random Fourier features and an exponential moving average. This approach was thoroughly evaluated by comparing it to 12 prominent algorithms for real-time anomaly detection on 12 diverse data streams.

A pivotal question arises when a court possesses information that an individual knows the passcode to a device. To answer this inquiry, we develop a novel approach to an established legal doctrine, drawing on precedents set by the case of Fisher v. US. Our theory enables us to prove that the government is incapable of forcing an individual to disclose the passcode, even if the court is certain the person has access to it. This concept is demonstrated through a specific scenario involving a user who has stored encrypted incriminating content on their device. The storage policy, as defined by the Electronic Communications Privacy Act, is explored to show that it is a function of both the user's knowledge of the decryption key and the device's capability to store encrypted data. By applying our theory to a scenario where the court is certain the user has access to the key, we show that the government is nonetheless precluded from compelling decryption.

We have developed a comprehensive model that enables simulation of the measurement-device-independent quantum key distribution (MDI-QKD) process. It can predict real-world observations and outcomes in scenarios involving linear channel loss, including the associated gain levels, error rates in different measurement bases, and final key rates. Our model is versatile and can be applied to various MDI-QKD implementations that employ convex source states or diverse coding techniques. As such, it is an invaluable resource for analyzing and evaluating the performance of different MDI-QKD protocols.

Researchers investigate polynomial-time approximation schemes (PTAS) for solving specific constraint satisfaction problems, such as Maximum Independent Set or Minimum Vertex Cover on graph classes that have limited connectivity.

A previously developed approach by Baker achieved PTAS on various graph classes including planar graphs. Further, Romero, Wrochna, and Zivny developed a simpler PTAS for certain graph classes using the Sherali-Adams LP relaxation for maximum CSPs with constraints defined by arbitrary non-negative polynomials.

This research is extended to CSPs with constraints defined by polynomials that have multiple values, such as Boolean constraints. A key challenge is addressing the issue of negative values, which involves introducing new variables and axioms to transform the original problem into a equivalent 0-1 linear programming problem.

The paper presents a simpler PTAS for general-valued CSPs with constraints that have specific properties, specifically those that only consider the combinations of variables that form a particular pattern, such as adjacent variables in a specific order. This achievement is also linked to a simpler PTAS for certain multi-graph classes with limited connectivity, specifically those where certain connected components are planar.

This study presents a novel, high-order numerical method for solving the linear Fokker-Planck equation under a constant diffusion term. The devised method integrates elements from the Lagrange-Galerkin and semi-Lagrangian techniques, yielding an explicit, conservative, consistent, and robust scheme capable of handling substantial time step sizes. A convergence analysis for the exactly integrated Lagrange-Galerkin approach is provided, along with an implementable alternative that employs approximate integration. The method is particularly useful in modeling time-dependent mean field games systems, enabling high-order solution approximations.

Advancements in machine learning and signal processing have generated substantial interest in Deep Neural Networks (DNNs), which excel at solving complex, engineering-driven problems. Nonetheless, employing such networks for critical life-altering decisions demands a deeper understanding of their decision-making processes. Unfortunately, most artificial neural networks, including DNNs, function as opaque systems, hindering insight into their internal workings. Although some research has initiated the quest to illuminate their behavior, the field of explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) remains underdeveloped. This study aims to offer a thorough exploration into comprehending, visualizing, and explicating the inner workings and global behavior of DNNs.

This study reveals intriguing evidence of a complex internal rotation pattern within a less massive and less luminous star that has evolved into a giant. Typically, lower and intermediate mass stars retain their rapid rotation rates during their main sequence phase. However, once these stars expand into giants, we expect a faster core rotation rate compared to their outer layers. Contrary to these expectations, KIC 9267654's rotation speed is observed to be higher near its surface rather than at its core, which presents a challenge to angular momentum conservation principles. To validate our findings, we updated the constraints based on spectroscopic surface measurements, verified that the detected oscillation patterns align with the previously determined core and outer layer rotation rates, and confirmed that the star exhibits no significant chemical abnormalities. Additionally, we eliminated the possibility of any interaction with a companion star that might be causing tidal forces. Lastly, we examined possible explanations, including an exchange of angular momentum with the star's core and outer layers due to tidal inertial waves generated by its rapid rotation, which could provide a temporary solution until more comprehensive theories become available.

Fake news has become a pressing concern on social media platforms due to its rapid dissemination and potential to cause harm worldwide. Although machine learning models have been trained for falsify news detection, they often struggle with new emerging patterns. This work introduces a novel FakeNews-Million dataset, comprising 1 million annotated samples, in order to address this challenge. Our proposed solution, the Meta Neural Process Networks model, excels in detecting fake news by leveraging prior knowledge and adapting to new information. This system combines the strengths of meta-learning and neural processes to effectively handle both existing and unfamiliar data. Experimental results indicate that our approach outperforms traditional models on the established benchmark datasets, like CNN and Char2016, as well as the newly introduced FakeNews-Million. Furthermore, our model showcases superior performance when confronted with newly created datasets, highlighting its capability to capture general, falsify-news characteristics.

This research paper examines a one-dimensional periodic transport equation featuring non-local flow and fractional decay. The equation in question is given by $$
u_{t}-(Hu)_{x}u_{x}+\kappa\Lambda^{\alpha}u=0,\quad (t,x)\in R^{+}\times S.
$$
Where $S$ denotes the domain, we have $\kappa\geq0$, $0<\alpha\leq1$, and investigate the well-posedness of this transport equation within $H^{3}(S)$ for a limited period of time. It is demonstrated that when $\kappa$ equals zero and the initial data is smooth and odd, the solution will eventually become singular over a finite period of time. Additionally, we find that introducing a weak dissipation term $\kappa\Lambda^{\alpha}u$ also leads to the formation of singularity in a finite amount of time.

This paper investigates the age of information (AoI) in a discrete-time status updating system that employs the Ber/G/1/1 queue. We demonstrate that utilizing a two-dimensional state vector which simultaneously monitors AoI and packet age enables derivation of the stationary AoI distribution via analysis of a constituted stochastic process. We present the general formula for the AoI distribution and derive an explicit expression for geometrically distributed service times. A comparison between discrete and continuous AoI time systems is also conducted, including derivation of the latter's parameters. We demonstrate that the standard continuous-time AoI formula can be applied to a specific scenario of geometrically distributed service times, yielding results that align with previously published research findings.

This work delves into various quantum algebras that arise from a special type of set-theoretic solution to the Yang-Baxter equation and their 'q-analogue' counterparts, also providing common characteristics that these algebras share in terms of quasi-bialgebras and twists. By establishing that set-theoretic and q-analogue solutions produce the same specific type of quasi-bialgebras, this research identifies an essential condition for any solution to yield a diagonalizable quantum group, specifically requiring that the permutation matrix be part of the solution's bialgebra structure. Furthermore, this finding leads to the creation of new solutions to the Yang-Baxter equation through the utilization of 6-dimensional non-diagonalizable quantum group twists, which itself cannot be expressed as a 1-dimensional twist of another quantum group.

Recently, Golay complementary matrices have gained popularity due to their utility in omnidirectional precoding techniques. This research extends Golay complementary matrices to higher-dimensional spaces known as multi-dimensional Golay complementary arrays and presents novel construction methods for pairs and quadruples of GCA. A set of ring identities is introduced to facilitate these constructions. Specifically, it is shown that GCA pairs are possible in four-dimensional space if certain conditions are met concerning the sizes and their factorization. Additionally, in binary GCM quadruples, possible sizes are postulated as unlimited, which is confirmed for sizes 78x78 and a few scattered instances, whereas a recently proposed method can also create a 390x390 GCM quad. A method is also provided to transform GCM pairs into GCM quadruples.

Quantum tunneling is an inherent process that lacks a direct analogy in classical physics, and it can compete with the finishing time of a full revival in highly entangled systems. By employing silicon quantum dots, this study delves into the realm of valleytronics, which utilizes the unique properties of hexagonal silicon to store and transmit information. Valley interference, a crucial phenomenon for quantum computing, is demonstrated on a graphene gate when the distance between silicon dots is minimized, a scenario that reduces spin exchange to a single atom. This research provides a foundation for the efficient execution of valley interference and spin exchange operations in silicon quantum technology.

Complex systems consisting of multiple interacting components typically adhere to straightforward and universal principles, which can be leveraged to achieve a deeper understanding by analyzing the interactions themselves. By transforming time-series data into a series of interconnected states using state-space reconstruction, our approach establishes a framework for extracting insights from complex systems. Utilizing this framework within a Graph Neural Network context allows us to investigate the impact of varying the number of measuring variables on our ability to recover the underlying dynamical structure and predict the system's future behavior.

We introduce an infinite family of recursive formulas for calculating the counts of binary integer partitions that fulfill specific divisibility criteria, establishing relationships among these counts via cumulative sums. These formulas have a meaningful interpretation within the framework of graded polynomial rings and enable us to derive computations related to homology modules in the context of stable homotopy theory, utilizing the properties of the mod $2$ Steenrod algebra.

A cutting-edge, minimally invasive therapy called Laser Interstitial Thermal Therapy (LITT) treats seizures caused by epilepsy in a specific brain area, the mesial temporal lobe. Evaluating the effectiveness of this treatment requires analyzing changes to the treated brain area after LITT, which can be achieved by accurately defining the treated region through image processing. Although deep learning techniques offer high precision in defining this region, training them requires a large amount of data which can be hard to obtain for a new and emerging treatment such as LITT. In response, this paper proposes an innovative framework called Progressive Brain Lesion Synthesis, consisting of multiple stages to artificially create more training data with various characteristics, thereby enhancing the precision of the therapy evaluation. Furthermore, the paper includes a design for encoding external information that can aid in training and improving segmentation results by integrating a condition and mask embedding block, resulting in better outcomes when compared to common image processing methods, according to experimental results.

Strong nonlocality, a phenomenon where systems demonstrate nonlocality without entanglement, can be seen in multipartite states with certain properties. Unextendible product bases (UPBs) have shown nonlocality without entanglement in previous research. Here, we examine UPBs in composite systems consisting of different types of qubits, focusing specifically on systems made of single qubits from different Hilbert spaces. Our main finding shows that strong nonlocality exists for UPBs in these systems, demonstrated through a series of UPBs with strong nonlocality in systems of two non-equivalent qubits. To achieve this, we developed an efficient method for identifying UPBs in these systems. Our research also explores relationships between UPBs in these systems and those in systems composed of equally capable qubits. To demonstrate strong nonlocality in action, we propose a series of closed-loop quantum circuits that generate strong nonlocality without requiring initial entanglement.

A breakthrough in robotics technology, astrobots are uniquely designed to coordinate fully independently with each other and the SDSS-V survey's transiting gas rich system targets. This innovative approach involves assigning unique spectral windows to each target, with potential overlaps between 10-20% of targets. To ensure safe and coordinated operations, astrobots employ a advanced risk assessment system, pinpointing potential electrical shocks, optical interference, and radio frequency disruptions. Through rigorous testing, our astrobots have demonstrated the capability to minimize risks below acceptable levels, with a 99.9% success rate in avoiding overlaps, and effective management of external interference factors. Furthermore, our analysis highlights the astrobots' ability to adapt to various stress scenarios, with a notable improvement in their resilience. With such exceptional safe coordination capabilities, the SDSS-V survey is poised to achieve a reduction of data system losses by a factor of ~100, allowing for a more sensitive detection of low-mass objects.

GP 2 is a graph-based language designed for efficient program analysis and verification, leveraging graph transformation rules to ease these tasks. However, efficiently developing GP 2 programs poses difficulties, primarily stemming from the time-consuming nature of graph matching. To overcome this limitation, the GP 2 framework incorporates a type of rooted rule that can be matched rapidly, given certain conditions are met. In order to accelerate the GP 2 compiler, several key modifications have been made to Bak's compiler found within the GP 2 framework. These modifications include using a more efficient data structure, optimizing code for better performance and ease of use, and introducing a command line interface that enables users to experiment with the compiler. Early test results indicate that the improved GP 2 compiler yields substantial speed improvements, achieving a rate of approximately 10 times faster than the original compiler.

Dimensionality reduction in high-dimensional data is effectively managed by feature extraction techniques, such as PCA and t-SNE. Self-supervised learning offers an alternative to traditional methods that rely on labeled data, using contrastive learning to extract valuable information about, extract key dimensions from high-dimensional data spaces. Our novel unified framework for feature extraction, inspired by contrastive learning, transforms data into more manageable forms with remarkable results, outperforming established methods in testing scenarios.

We establish an infinite sequence of locally arc-transitive graphs characterized by a unique property: their automorphism groups partition vertices into two distinct orbits while exhibiting quasiprimativity on just one orbit, specifically within a class of twisted wreath structures. Our findings expand upon a framework initially proposed by Giudici, Li, and Praeger by providing an infinite number of examples classified under the star normal quotient twisted wreath category for locally arc-transitive graphs.

Working with categorical data for model selection and sparse modeling becomes increasingly complex as the number of variables grows, as it typically requires a parameter for each category, making interpretation challenging. Despite its efficiency for handling continuous and categorical variables, the Group Lasso often results in inconsistent estimates, rendering the model difficult to interpret due to the lack of sparsity. To achieve a sparse solution using the Group Lasso, we propose a two-step method: first reducing data dimensions through the Group Lasso, and then employing an information criterion on a subset of clustered models. This algorithm's performance is evaluated under high-dimensional conditions and compared with state-of-the-art methods using synthetic and real-world datasets, showing its superior performance in terms of prediction accuracy and model size.

Recent advances in large language models have achieved human-like performance on numerous language tasks. However, the potential for these models to effectively utilize structured information, particularly within knowledge graphs, compared to free-form text, has not been extensively explored. To bridge this knowledge gap, our approach develops a method to incorporate structured knowledge into LLMs through training on specific knowledge graph triples. We demonstrate that LLMs pre-trained with our technique on a vast knowledge base like Wikidata outperform conventional T5 models in various evaluation benchmarks. Specifically, our approach shows comparable performance when compared to training models on descriptive language containing the same information, and significantly improves performance when utilizing smaller knowledge graphs. One key advantage of this method is the absence of requirement for costly human-annotated data during training.

This article examines spatially nonlocal diffusion models, where interactions are limited to a finite distance $\delta$ and investigates how they are defined in a bounded area with various boundary conditions representing inhomogeneous data. The article compares their solutions with classical PDE models under specific localization limits, as well as how rescaled fractional kernels relate to inhomogeneous fractional boundary value problems. These discussions shed light on the challenges and issues that arise in nonlocal problems with inhomogeneous data within bounded domains.

When capturing panoramic scenes, individuals usually align their cameras parallel to gravity's direction. This research focuses on serving high-quality, wide-angle image material for training deep learning-based models, specifically those of CNNs, by tackling the challenge of stitching partial, panoramic images. A unique approach has been proposed, leveraging a single feature map to combine images by averaging matching features along the direction perpendicular to alignment, thus ensuring a smooth, unified image. This method's efficiency yields real-time processing, ensuring smooth integration of images, and effectively handling scenes with dark areas, rigid transformations, and mild occlusions. Moreover, the proposed framework's potential applications extend beyond image stitching, also implying a method for consolidating partial views for 3D reconstruction, as demonstrated through various experiments and comparisons with existing techniques.

Hanzer and Muić's work on degenerate Eisenstein series cancellations has been built upon, 
extending their method and outcome to a specific set of Eisenstein series, 
specifically those formed from the combinations of two Speh representations 
$\Delta(\tau,m)|\cdot|^{s_1}\otimes\Delta(\tau,n)|\cdot|^{s_2}$ in $GL(m+n,\mathbb{A}_\mathbb{Q})$ for self-dual cuspidal automorphic representation $\tau$.

This study develops a novel biophysical brain model for areas associated with Parkinson's disease, utilizing local field potential data obtained from marmoset monkey brains. Parkinson's disease, a neurodegenerative disorder caused by the death of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra, disrupts normal basal ganglia-thalamus-cortex function. Despite multiple contributing mechanisms, a comprehensive explanation and effective cure for the disease remain elusive. In response to this gap, computational models incorporating aspects of animal models have been suggested. Our model leverages a data-driven strategy to optimize parameters with a differential evolution method. Successful outcomes from the evolved models closely matched observed firing rates and spectral characteristics of local field potentials from healthy and diseased state data. Furthermore, results from the evolved models accurately replicated key features observed during deep brain stimulation. This research offers a starting point for further refinement and expansion of the model to explore multiple pathways contributing to Parkinson's disease progression.

Achieving a seamless visual experience and optimal system performance when displaying line joins on vector maps requires an efficient anti-aliasing technique. However, the limitations of OpenGL and OpenGL ES in rendering 2D graphics led to the development of a novel algorithm utilizing RGBA buffers and stencil buffers to effectively minimize disk reads and memory copies. The devised method, utilizing RGBA and stencil buffers through blitting and GPGPU techniques, has been found particularly beneficial for map displays involving large numbers of lines at high frame rates. Furthermore, user interaction with line joins is facilitated through update capabilities. The proposed technique has been successfully implemented and tested across multiple platforms and operating systems.

Our team utilized the KOOLS-IFU on Seimei Telescope for integral field unit (IFU) observations of 9 ultra/luminous infrared galaxies located close to our own (z < 0.04) and participating in the GOALS survey. These targets span a broad spectrum of merger phases, from early stages to advanced. With the IFU data we collected, we successfully isolated several distinct emission lines including hydrogen beta, oxygen III at wavelength 5007, hydrogen alpha, double-ionized nitrogen at wavelengths 6549, 6583, and sulfur II at wavelengths 6717, 6731. Our analysis with spectral resolutions ranging between 1500 to 2000 allowed us to derive spatially resolved ionized gas maps as well as their corresponding spectra. Preliminary examinations with long-slit observations and modeling using binary masks suggest that the IFU data holds substantial value in understanding the ionized gas components in these galaxies. We are now prepared to engage in in-depth analyses with our full IFU datasets.

The multivariate interpolation operator is traditionally constructed using piecewise linear functions to approximate absolute differences between values. In this study, we develop a novel, transcendental interpolation function derived from the hyperbolic tangent, providing more precise approximations of functions that increase linearly with the distance. Building on the Wu-Schaback quasi-interpolation formula, we adapt this new interpolation function while preserving the original scheme's characteristics, including monotonicity and convexity. It has been mathematically proven that our adaptation converges at a rate of O(h^2), enabling smoother interpolation results. Several numerical experiments are presented to demonstrate the method's efficiency and accuracy.

Transportation systems are frequently hindered by unpredictable weather conditions.
Current methods of weather prediction, using either a network of sensors or a vehicle-mounted camera, are limited in scope and costly.
A robust weather detection system is crucial for seamless operation of transportation services in diverse weather conditions.
However, this task is complex due to the varied nature of weather and the scarcity of distinct characteristics that distinguish different weather conditions.
Existing approaches to this problem are largely confined to specific environments and only tackle the classification of two weather types.
In this study, we introduce the RFS dataset, which includes images representing three categories of weather (rain, snow, and fog), and propose a novel algorithm utilizing super-pixel masks for data augmentation to yield satisfactory results using multiple Convolutional Neural Network configurations.

To improve modeling long sequences in the time domain for speech separation, a dual-path RNN was previously proposed by dividing lengthy sequences into shorter chunks and processing them with internal and external RNN components. Building upon this work, a Dual-Path Convolution Recurrent Network (DPCRN) model is presented here by integrating the dual-path RNN with Convolution Recurrent Networks. The model's RNN components were substituted with dual-path modules where internal components were used to analyze single-frame spectral patterns, and external components were used to analyze consecutive frame dependencies. Notably, with only 0.8 million parameters, the DPCRN model achieved an overall mean opinion score (MOS) of 3.57 in the wideband scenario of the Interspeech 2021 DNS challenge. Evaluations across additional datasets have shown the efficacy of this model.

A new statistics method is introduced, focusing on the turn-around radii of cluster halos to break the degeneracy between $\Lambda$CDM, alternative $f(R)$ gravity models, and massive neutrinos cosmologies. By analyzing the rockstar halo catalogs at the present day from the DUSTGRAIN-pathfinder $N$-body simulations, this work distinguishes between $f(R)$ gravity with standard neutrino masses and the scenario with massive neutrinos within $\Lambda$CDM. It is discovered that f(R) gravity models generally yield larger turn-around radii, whereas massive neutrinos generally result in smaller radii. A distinct separation between the two alternative cosmologies is found through the distribution of turn-around radii in the $\xi$-$r_t$ plane. The predicted number counts of ultra-distant, massive quasars can be estimated using the four-parameter extension of the $f(R)$ gravity - massive neutrinos model.

Recently introduced multi-fluid models hold promise in refining the simulation of atmospheric convection within weather and climate simulations. A dynamic framework by nature, this method eliminates several of the mass-flux convection scheme's assumptions that are no longer valid at modern model resolution levels. Nonetheless, research into the multi-fluid approach is in its initial stages. The present study seeks to contribute to the development of this new framework by testing a two-fluid model applied to Rayleigh-Benard convection. The model's fluids represent air and a warmer, less dense substance resembling water vapour that's present in the atmosphere's lower layers. The researcher utilized the model to analyze convection under increasingly unstable conditions and discovered that the traditional approach to describing atmospheric convection - characterized by a linear relationship between heat flux and lapse rate - holds true only when the conditions are near neutral. The study indicates that the traditional approach may lose accuracy when dealing with highly unstable or stable conditions, which is where atmospheric convection becomes particularly complex and robust models are needed to capture its dynamics accurately.

We investigate three separate Jaynes-Cummings systems, with two of the systems having correlated atoms, but the third system is unconnected. Our goal is to identify when this unconnected system could genuinely become entangled with the others. Our analysis shows that it is impossible if the unconnected system's cavity shares classical correlations with another cavity. Conversely, the unconnected system's state may become genuinely multipartite entangled if its cavity is highly entangled with another cavity, offering a novel method for creating multipartite entanglement via JC-interactions. Furthermore, this finding can be experimentally realized using existing setups.

The Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) is one of the experiments that occupies the largest portion of the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) at CERN. As part of the CMS upgrade for the High Luminosity Large Hadron Collider (HL-LHC), the CMS has replaced its existing detector components with more advanced and upgraded versions. The online data collection for the CMS will be provided by the Trigger System, which must deliver this information at the rate of 100 GB/s. The CMS has opted for a two-level approach in its Trigger System. The first level, also known as the L1, utilizes the Full Detector Data (FDD) to achieve this rate, while the second level, or the L2, relies on the information from the front-end detectors. The latter has been moved from the FDD. Both L1 and L2 are responsible for gathering information from the entire detector and deciding which events contain potential physics. The increased complexity of the process has made it necessary to test the data transfer and reconstruction processes for the upgraded detector components. The pilot blades of the CMS silicon pixel detector (PSI) were used for this purpose as they feature new readout electronics and a more efficient data transfer approach compared to the existing ones. This paper presents the results of the reconstruction process of the pilot blades and discusses their associated challenges.

A method is presented for computing the Kall\'en-Lehmann spectral density from lattice QCD data, which remains gauge invariant. The proposed method is tested on the SU(2) glueball spectrum for specific quantum numbers and at varying lattice spacings. The study employs published data to determine the spectral density and the glueball spectrum. The results for the ground state mass are consistent with the conventional approach using exponential correlations. Additionally, preliminary indications of excited states within the spectrum can be derived from the spectral density.

Social media monitoring through sentiment analysis on platforms like Twitter enables
organizations and individuals to track the public's emotions towards them and their rivals.
As a result, analyzing public sentiment has become both crucial and difficult to accomplish.
In this project, we gathered and manually annotated seven freely accessible Twitter sentiment
databases. We then compiled a new set of training and testing data from these sources. An
LSTM-based classification model was developed to determine the sentiment expressed in each
annotation. The model's performance was assessed using the newly created dataset.

A nonlinear interaction occurs between electromagnetic fields in quantum electrodynamics, resulting in vacuum polarization. This interaction can lead to a new field of non-linear electrodynamics that affects black hole physics, including black hole solutions and their thermal properties. In this research, a non-linear charged AdS black hole was developed and its thermal properties, including entropy and temperature, were found to be influenced by the Weyl anomaly. Building on the work of Tawaki and Takayama, we model the anisotropic distribution of quantum fields on the black hole's horizon using the Proca theory's stress-energy tensor. The result shows that the anisotropy contributes to a shift in the temperature and entropy of the non-linear charged AdS black hole. This finding can provide a non-linear electrodynamics framework for understanding thermal properties in black hole physics.

Reconstructing a quantum state of continuous-variable systems from partial knowledge of their Wigner function is known as quantum state tomography. Research has shown that certain features of an optical tomogram are directly linked to an entropy-based quantity used to measure the degree of entanglement in a two-mode state. A key finding of this research is the identification of specific optical tomogram phases that serve as indicators of both entanglement and the onset of synchronization in a system of coupled oscillators.

Recent advances in open-domain dialogue models have achieved significant breakthroughs.
Despite this, developing a scalable chat system poses a major challenge due to
the requirement for substantial human-human dialogue data to support features
like persona, style, or safety. To tackle this issue, our work aims to introduce
role constraints to open-domain dialogue systems that enable them to consistently
maintain assigned roles during human conversations. Achieving this involves
defining a role specification with specific criteria for stated features and
policies on allowed types of utterances. To build this system efficiently, we
propose a framework for collecting data that leverages few-shot learning from
large language models, thereby enabling the creation of role-compliant dialogue
datasets from scratch. Furthermore, we examine various open-domain dialogue
system architectures in terms of their ability to meet role specifications and
maintain natural conversation. Results from both automatic and human evaluations
reveal that our models perform satisfactorily in terms of role conformance, while
still delivering competitive performance on overall conversational metrics.

Farmers utilize pesticides to minimize crop losses, but their effectiveness often depends on analyzing average treatment benefits and risks. Evaluating pesticide efficacy using certainty equivalents and ranking treatment efficiency through stochastic efficiency is a common practice. However, the major drawback of this approach is collecting a sufficient number of observations for statistically meaningful results. Since field experiments typically have a limited number of replicated trials, the results lack sufficient data. Moreover, the conventional method solely considers farmer profitability, disregarding the influence of disease pressure on yields and profit. To address these challenges, we developed a method using simulations to account for a limited number of observations and incorporated disease pressure into yield and profit functions through a logical model. We applied this method to investigate the efficacy of organic disease management practices on strawberry fields. The results showed that the method was an effective way to evaluate treatment efficiency even with a limited number of replicated trials and accounted for the significant impact of disease pressure on yields and profit.

360-degree streaming videos offer engaging and immersive experiences, allowing viewers to control the viewpoint through navigation methods like clicking, dragging, and tapping on subtitles displayed at the bottom of the screen. However, managing and maintaining quality in such videos can be very challenging, especially when they are publicly shared without headings or indexes. Our proposed approach provides accurate viewpoint prediction based on user clicking behavior in 360-degree streaming videos. A database featuring subtitles mapped to viewing directions is created through analysis of video data, which is utilized in our framework. Testing of our approach on real video data demonstrates its precision and effectiveness, outperforming existing methods. Our system is user-friendly, providing interactive features such as subtitle display and viewpoint adjustment, enhancing the viewing experience.

Tensor network methods have commonly been utilized in modeling different types of equilibrium and non-equilibrium situations. However, these techniques faced a critical challenge as their algorithms generally necessitated a small bond dimension at sufficiently low temperatures or time points, despite a fundamental requirement for approximating thermal states and time-evolved systems where the bond dimension is directly related to system size. This issue was tackled by constructing a specific class of objects that are able to accurately represent the thermal expectation values and time-evolved behavior for local observables in any scenario, where the bond dimension is completely independent of the system's size and is only determined by the temperature or elapsed time. Furthermore, we demonstrate the applicability of these constructed objects in approximating thermal correlations and expectation values following a quantum quench event.

We develop a decoupling theory for a diverse range of high-order smooth surfaces in three-dimensional space without planar components. Our approach can also handle surfaces described by non-uniform polynomial equations. By examining these surfaces, we create an opportunity to adapt and expand the concept of linear decoupling, incorporating techniques like Taylor series approximation and subsequent analysis of surface-based approximations. Our findings demonstrate that when a surface approximation method has a clear, well-defined form - even if it is complicated - it can still facilitate decoupling, provided the method meets specific criteria. We further demonstrate that our results can be applied to resolve unresolved issues within the field of decoupling and that our theorems can be used to tackle a broader range of problems involving smooth, three-dimensional space.

In this research, we establish a precise inequality relating anisotropic mean curvature and capacity in the L^p norm, applicable to any bounded area in R^n with smooth borders.
As a result, we derive inequalities including an anisotropic Willmore inequality, a sharp anisotropic Minkowski inequality, and a sharp volumetric anisotropic Minkowski inequality. Our proof involves a novel approach in nonlinear potential theory recently described in the reference provided.

The Microscope space test for the weak equivalence principle involves measuring tiny differences in the acceleration of two test masses as they orbit the Earth. Violations of this principle would appear as specific frequencies related to the satellite's movement. This experiment was designed to minimize potential errors at these critical frequencies. Unforeseen acceleration fluctuations known as glitches can impact test mass acceleration readings, likely caused by cracks in the satellite's protective layer. These events, which are relatively short-lived, have an intrinsic randomness to them. While they seem random, the time of their occurrence is influenced by the satellite's orbital and spinning cycles. It is crucial to understand the effect glitches have on the principle test, but the current data isn't sufficient for a conclusive determination. As a result, the most reliable approach to minimize their influence is to exclude data from periods with detected glitches.

We examine a rigid structure composed of two active Brownian particles that interact in an activity gradient. We demonstrate analytically that the position of the dimer varies based on the angle between the particles and accumulates either at areas with high activity levels or low activity levels. This corresponds to chemotaxis and antichemotaxis respectively. Some dimer configurations display chemotactic and antichemotactic properties, with their behavior determined by the activity gradient strength. A coarsely detailed approach helps to generate an effective potential, used in our analysis to create a phase diagram. This diagram classifies dimer configurations based on their tactic behavior and also indicates how some dimers can maintain direction and achieve greater persistence in motion. This study provides valuable insights into the design of autonomous, responsive colloidal systems that can navigate according to varying activity levels in their environment.

The minimum strong shortest path cover with k-hops in a graph G is the smallest number of sets needed among all k-hops strong shortest path covers, where we also examine 2-hops covers for certain graphs and show the general k-hops cover problem is NP-complete.

The impact of infrared renormalons in the color dipole gluon distribution's variance is being quantified, and calculations demonstrate how non-linear small-x saturation impacts shift the Borel plane's initial IR pole from $2/\beta_2$ to $1/\beta_2$, thereby changing the estimated uncertainty to approximately $\Lambda_{\rm QCD}^2$ instead of $\Lambda_{\rm QCD}^4$.

As the number of frogs per site grows, the frog model's behavior shifts from transient to recurrent on a d-ary rooted tree. We demonstrate that this critical transition occurs roughly around the tree's degree.

Researchers are focusing on extremely thin alloys made of rare earth and transition metals, with controlled composition and unique magnetic properties, to create advanced photonic applications that operate rapidly. Despite the potential, it is very difficult to achieve small scale dimensions, which are essential for scaling down devices, due to difficulties in growth methods. This study demonstrates a breakthrough by integrating rare earth and transition metals at the surface of a titanium alloy without mixing at the alloy level. When exposed to light, this surface layer reacts quickly, allowing for precise control of magnetic properties and a significant shift in optical properties that can be adjusted by aligning the light source in different directions. This discovery enables development of rare earth transition metal alloys that can control light and magnetic fields with high precision, paving the way for faster photonic technology.

Knowledge distillation is a successful method for efficiently training a compact neural network by imitating the behavior of a larger pre-trained model. Traditionally, having access to the pre-trained model's weights is necessary for this process. In this research, the possibility of knowledge distillation is explored when the pre-trained model is inaccessible, with only its decision-making capabilities available for query. Under this scenario, we develop a framework that utilizes decision-based queries to extract features from the black-box model and utilizes these features to train a target model with minimal labels. The effectiveness of this approach is validated across various scenarios and network architectures, and it demonstrates the potential to achieve comparable performance to model-assisted knowledge distillation. Furthermore, our approach's versatility is showcased by successfully adapting it to a zero-shot scenario, achieving notable improvements over conventional distillation methods.

Researchers have observed the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_S$ decay mode for the first time, and have also gathered evidence for the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_S$ decay mode, utilizing a 3.0 $\text{fb}^{-1}$ dataset of $pp$ collisions collected at 7 and 8 TeV center-of-mass energies by the LHCb. The branching fractions for these decays are calculated as follows: The $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 \bar{K}^0$ branching fraction is estimated at (4.3±0.5±0.3±0.3±0.6) ×10^-4, and the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} \bar{K}^0$ branching fraction is estimated at (2.8±1.0±0.3±0.2±0.4) ×10^-4, with the given uncertainties stemming from various sources.

Constructing the lattice of submodules of a given module is generally a challenging task. Despite the proposed method by Stanley to construct distributive lattices from their join irreducibles, determining all join irreducible submodules of a given module is not a straightforward task. However, for modules that have no module composition multiplicities, we present an alternative approach based on the composition factors, drawing on the theory of ordered sets to determine all join irreducible submodules and construct the lattice of submodules.

A strong geodetic subset of a graph~$G$ comprises a selection of vertices~$S$, which allows for the coverage of the remaining vertices in~$G$, by establishing unique shortest paths between all pairs of vertices in~$S$. The Strong Geodetic problem (SG) involves determining if a graph~$G$ and an integer~$k$ have a subset of vertices~$S$, with at most~$k$ elements, which is strong geodetic. This problem has been proven to be NP-hard for all graphs. This study introduces the Strong Geodetic Recognition problem (SGR), which requires identifying if a specific vertex subset~$S$ within a graph~$G$ constitutes a strong geodetic subset. SGR is found to be NP-complete. Research into SGR is conducted, and comparisons of computational complexities are made across various graph types, including the derivation of efficient algorithms, NP-completeness proofs, and preliminary results on parameterized complexity, which provide insight into the complexity of SG, particularly in chordal graphs.

We tackle the challenge of efficient imitation learning from an imperfect training set, focusing on the common issue that experts may not provide a perfect policy when labeling states. To bridge this gap, we develop a novel algorithm called TRAIL that leverages both expert feedback and a second, lower-quality source: a high-performance policy derived from state visits during pre-training. By combining these sources, TRAIL enables near-optimal learning with significantly reduced labeling costs. Key advantages include: (1) TRAIL can exploit a suboptimal labeling distribution without suffering a corresponding decrease in performance, (2) it offers a way to flexibly trade off expert labels against state visits, and (3) it extends the potential benefits of imitation learning to broader sets of states that have been experienced during pre-training. Through theoretical and empirical evaluations, we show that TRAIL achieves significantly better performance than both expert-only imitation learning and learning-only from the suboptimal policy.

Reinforcement learning efficiency can be significantly enhanced through imitation learning by leveraging expert guidance. However, relying on expert demonstrations is often impractical or too costly due to the high expense of gathering them. In this research, we introduce a pioneering Co-Imitation Learning framework to circumvent this issue. CoIL leverages peer agents' successful experiences by training two distinct agents in an alternating exploration-exploitation process. Although agent experiences may be both beneficial and misleading, our method employs value function expected gain estimation to filter out less useful knowledge. As a result, the agents learn from each other, selectively imitating valuable information and rejecting unnecessary data. Experimentation across multiple scenarios highlights the superiority of our Co-Imitation Learning framework, confirming the benefits of inter-agent knowledge exchange in the absence of external supervision.

This work presents a metric function that yields an optimal bound of $n-h(\delta \epsilon) - 1$ bits for the storage capacity of a quantum channel with an error rate of $\delta \epsilon$ for a specific type of code, specifically PAC codes from the work of Haukkanen, Korrapati, and Kerenidis (PRL 123, 150501, 2019) that combine the benefits of polar codes and code concatenation. Unlike existing metrics such as the quantum multiple-access bound (QMAB) with a storage capacity of $n-h(\delta \epsilon)$ - 1, our approach provides a specific capacity value for any error rate $\delta \epsilon$ without relying on polar code design, allowing it to be compared to the storage capacity of single-qubit channels with the same error rate. For the first time, our approach shows that the storage capacity of a tri-qubit GHZ state with a mixed state error rate $\delta \epsilon$ is less than 2 - 2$h(\delta \epsilon)$. Our approach also enables us to derive a tighter upper limit for the storage capacity of PAC codes with an error rate of $\delta \epsilon$, specifically $1-h(\delta \epsilon) - \frac{1-h(\delta \epsilon))^2}{4}$, which is comparable to the QMAB upper limit and demonstrates that the storage capacity of a single-qubit GHZ state with an error rate of $\

Using reinforcement learning post maximum likelihood estimation pre-training can significantly improve neural machine translation efficiency. Nonetheless, a notable issue with RL for NMT arises from the large action space hindering its performance, as our hypothesis proposes. We've conducted series of experiments which support this assumption and showcase its consequences across various setup variations including different model sizes, bilingual corpora, and language pairs. Subsequent experiments demonstrate our proposed solution - compressing the action space - which yields substantial improvements in translation accuracy, as verified across diverse evaluation metrics and data conditions. Our findings facilitate the smooth integration of RL into NMT systems, thus offering practical pathways for enhancing NMT models through RL methods.

A novel, markerless extrinsic calibration system is introduced that relies on real-world depth camera data rather than simulation or fiducial markers. Our system leverages machine learning to automatically develop and utilize real-world models for identifying and positioning the end-effector, predicting object poses, and determining critical points necessary for object manipulation. A specific algorithm was developed and tested for a particular end-effector, but the system's framework is versatile and adaptable to various end-effectors and objects. Results from repeated experiments using a fixed setup and configuration demonstrated an average pose estimation error of 0.48 cm, with a maximum error of 0.76 cm, and a median rotation error of 1.45 degrees, with a range of 1.45 to 3.14 degrees.

This study introduces two key concepts, quasi-finitely separating maps and quasiapproximate identities, which form the basis for the definitions of QFS-spaces and quasicontinuous maps. Building upon these definitions, various properties and characteristics of QFS-spaces are investigated. Key findings include: Firstly, any QFS-space is inherently a quasicontinuous space; secondly, closed subspaces, as well as quasicontinuous projection spaces, derived from QFS-spaces, are themselves QFS-spaces; thirdly, continuous retracts of QFS-spaces possess the same characteristic and specific types of QFS-space retracts can be constructed; lastly, upper power spaces of continuous QFS-spaces correspond to FS-spaces.

The rise of partisanship seems to be rising across various metrics including voter behavior and online engagement. Research into the Web's influence on polarization has produced several key findings in the past. To build on existing research and gain deeper insights, we've studied browsing habits of thousands of users along with their online interactions with news sources. Our results reveal that users' online exposure to news sources follows distinct ideological patterns where they consistently spend more time browsing news aligned with their own viewpoint. Moreover, we've identified clear partisan groups within the broader online population based on shared browsing habits. Ultimately, we examined the impact of user decision-making on online polarization, and we've uncovered substantial evidence indicating users' deliberate actions can contribute significantly to the amplification of partisan divisions.

We examine the Lehnert and Schweitzer proof that the word problem for Thompson's group V has a non-context-free property. We further prove this word problem to be equivalent to the complement of the cyclic suffix of the rational subset generated by V's identity, and demonstrate a higher complexity level, specifically $\not\subseteq \text{DTIME}(n^2)$, for its decision variant.

The study of open quantum systems under periodic driving forces is highly captivating 
because, in most cases, they achieve a non-equilibrium steady state, which is
marked by a constant current. In this study, we examine a situation where a
single photon is used to gate an isolated qubit, and this process is repeated.
However, we found that, instead of a steady state, the system enters a periodic
transient state due to the driven nature of the system. This occurs when the
period of driving is longer than the system's relaxation time. This phenomenon
can be understood through a theoretical approach that uses a periodic steady state
projection superoperator. Ultimately, our experiment and theory provide a clear
understanding of the challenges involved in achieving a non-equilibrium steady
state in a driven system.

We explore how several established recurrent operators including curvature, Ricci, Jacobi, shape, and Weyl operators contribute substantially to biharmonic hypersurfaces being minimal within the Euclidean space.

A rational number p/q represents the basis for a numbering system. Words composed of digits 0 through p-1 in base p/q correspond to unique rational numbers, which make up the set Np/q. While previous studies on base p/q systems focus on evaluating words that translate to nonnegative integers, our analysis examines subsets of (Np/q)d that are identifiable using finite automata in (Ap)d. Our initial contribution identifies the subsets defined by first-order logic similar to those defined by the Bachi-Bruyere Theorem in integer base systems. Furthermore, our findings demonstrate that both natural order relation and modulo-q operator cannot be expressed by finite automata in base p/q systems.

Adding three right-handed neutrinos and a simple QCD axion sector to the Standard Model effectively explains multiple phenomena including neutrino oscillations, dark matter, and baryon asymmetry. In doing so, it resolves the strong CP problem and addresses the cosmological dark matter enigma. This model also facilitates the creation of sterile neutrinos at the GeV scale, satisfying constraints from both laboratory experiments and astrophysical observations. As a result, it offers a comprehensive explanation for all dark matter phenomena.
