This effect is caused by the ongoing competition between two speed factors: the rate at which the particles reassemble, which is influenced by forces like viscosity and surface tension, and the rate at which the raft is stretched apart by its boundaries. This conflict ultimately decides the length of cracks that form within the raft. Interestingly, if we instead stretch a raft very quickly, its pattern of breakdown changes to match that of a material with fixed pieces that are only connected at their boundaries, indicating that the reassembly of the particles has been paused by the speed of the stretching.

We've analyzed a range of SU(Nc) gauge theories in 3D lattices that incorporate degenerate, multi-component complex scalar fields. These scalar fields are part of the fundamental representation of both the SU(Nc) gauge group and the global U(Nf) symmetry group. We've investigated their interactions within a general quartic potential that is compatible with the global and gauge symmetries. By analyzing minimum-energy configurations and performing Monte Carlo simulations, we've studied the phase diagrams, Higgs phases, and corresponding symmetry-breaking patterns. The influence of the quartic potential has also been considered. Additionally, we explored whether lattice model transitions relate to the behavior of continuum field theory at its stable charged fixed points, specifically using Kosterlitz-Nishimura-Hamame-Nishimura statistics to compare coupling constants and using the impact of the quartic potential to relate degenerate directions to the universal features of the 2D Coulomb phase.

Our novel TD learning approach overcomes several challenges robots encounter when navigating underwater.  By leveraging Gaussian Process regression, our method significantly boosts data efficiency by limiting TD updates.  To facilitate online predictions, we developed a new sparse approximation technique with enhanced performance compared to current rejection-based methods.  By deriving the posterior of the value function and utilizing its moments, we developed SPGP-SARSA: a new algorithm for offline policy evaluation.  Our results show that SPGP-SARSA outperforms the existing state-of-the-art in sparse methods and matches the accuracy of its precise equivalent while successfully being applied to underwater navigation.  Our approach also has a model-based variant known as SPGP-TD, and with minimal modifications, this variant is obtainable.  Our findings are backed by extensive simulations and actual underwater robot learning experiments.

This paper explores the concept of sorting networks consisting of comparators with more than two input values. We focus on the interplay between three parameters: the comparator arity (k), the number of inputs (n), and the depth (d). Our model has significant relevance, as studying it helps us comprehend the inner workings of sorting networks on (k, n)-meshes, a data structure commonly employed in computer architecture and parallel computation. In this paper, we investigate the parameter trade-offs, especially seeking to understand what arities are necessary for achieving minimal depth in sorting networks. Through our analysis and constructions, we identify essential properties for a network to be of minimal depth, and we demonstrate that, given sufficient depth, many comparator arities can be utilized simultaneously. Ultimately, this allows us to devise a sorting network that employs comparators with any arity between 2 and n, and our results on this strategy are applicable across a broad range of comparator arities. Furthermore, our results encompass both small and large comparator inputs, and they demonstrate that the choice of sorting network becomes increasingly robust as comparators handle more input values.

We employ a 1+1+2 covariant semi-tetrad method to describe a static and spherically symmetric relativistic star comprising two fluids with anisotropic pressures, leading to the derivation of anisotropic Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff equations in covariant form. By direct resolution and transformation, new expressions for the anisotropic potentials are derived, offering explicit solutions subject to specific boundary conditions mirroring those of the standard isotropic case.

Using recent observations, we create a set of realistic models for a galaxy like the Milky Way. By combining four different components - a central bulge, bar, four spiral arms, and a weak outer disk - we run extensive simulations to study their interactions. Our findings show that a bar with medium length causes a weak outer disk and four distinct spiral arms; shorter bars instead result in an outer disk broken into two arms, while longer bars produce an outer disk broken into three arms. The distribution of star forming regions follows the pattern seen in observations, with higher rates in the spiral arms and a lower rate in the bulge. The majority of supernovae occur in low-mass star forming regions within the disk. Our simulations also show that a bar with medium length affects the motion of globular clusters in the central region, whereas shorter bars increase the velocity of these clusters. This research provides a foundation for further studies on the bar's formation and evolution, as well as the creation of realistic models for other galaxies.

Galactic mergers significantly shape galaxy evolution, especially those involving massive galaxy combinations that significantly alter galaxy morphology. This study focuses on how magnetic fields affect major mergers involving abundant gas, using high-resolution simulations to examine the impact. Conducting this analysis within a realistic cosmic framework, this work employs advanced numerical tools to model magnetic fields' effects on galaxy interactions. Results show that magnetic fields weaken the massive dynamical processes associated with galaxy mergers, resulting in more orderly galaxy movements and less distorted galaxy shapes. Furthermore, star formation patterns are significantly altered, with magnetic fields shifting the peak to earlier stages due to the more efficient formation of stars in gas collapses. Additionally, this study finds that magnetic fields help maintain galaxy discs' structure by suppressing the formation of massive stars that would otherwise be scattered by gravitational forces, leading to a desire to investigate the impact on galaxy formation more broadly.

Our solution to the 2nd COVID-19 Severity Detection Competition has been successfully presented, where our goal was to classify chest CT images into Mild, Moderate, Severe, and Critical COVID-19 grades. To achieve this, we proposed a cutting-edge infection-aware 3D classification network called the Contrastive Mixup Classification network. This innovative approach involved initially training two segmentation networks to identify lung regions and inner lesions. These lesion masks were used in conjunction with the original CT scans to generate additional useful information. To rectify data imbalance, we incorporated weighted cross-entropy loss and over-sampled the under-represented severe cases. The pre-trained network was then fine-tuned on reduced-dose CT scans with adapted lesion masks, enabling the detection of COVID-19 severity on low-dose CT scans with poor image quality. Consequently, our approach earned the top rank on the final leader board with a critical case accuracy rate of 24.5%, significantly outperforming the competition in the critical case category and surpassing the best baseline score in the moderate and severe case categories.

Most current sequence-to-sequence based Grammatical Error Correction methods focus primarily on generating more pseudo data to improve performance. In contrast, little work addresses the challenge of adapting GEC to new domains with limited resources. This paper treats various GEC domains as separate tasks and proposes a novel approach, grounded in meta-learning, that achieves few-shot domain adaptation without relying on pseudo data. Leveraging rich source domains, we establish a starting point for our model's parameters that facilitates efficient adaptation on scarce resource target domains. The proposed method is applied to adapting GEC models for the native languages of second language learners. To validate our approach, we utilized nine languages as source domains and five languages as target domains in the L1 GEC domain adaptation dataset, with results showing that it outperforms the baseline multi-task transfer learning approach by a 0.50 F score on average and enables successful adaptation to entirely new target domains (e.g., Vietnamese) for the first time.

Rounding is an essential concept used extensively in research, business, and everyday life. A commonly employed method involves rounding numerical values to the nearest whole number, a technique known as "rounding to the nearest integer." In this study, a novel probability distribution, dubbed the offset Poisson, is introduced to model situations where the actual count is an integer rounded to the nearest whole number. Offset Poisson models can be utilized to analyze over/under reports, estimate genuine counts, and assess distribution properties through rounded data. In addition, this research demonstrates that standard statistical testing approaches may yield inaccurate results when dealing with rounded data and recommends employing joint maximum likelihood estimation. The proposed models are illustrated using real-world data sets, including British household cat ownership statistics and NCAA basketball shooting accuracy records.

Researchers investigated the crystal and magnetic characteristics of the single-crystal, hexagonal GdInO3 through an integrated approach that combined experimental and theoretical analysis. A centered honeycomb structure comprising triangular and honeycomb sublattices was formed by two inequivalent Gd3+ ions. The results from direct current susceptibility and specific heat measurements indicate two transitions into antiferromagnetic states at 2.3 K and 1.02 K. Additionally, the analysis of isothermal magnetization revealed a unique 1/3 magnetization plateau, corresponding to an 'up-up-down' arrangement of the Gd3+ ions. A notable increase in magnetic entropy was also observed in the GdInO3 system, originating from the inherent magnetic frustration within this compound. A model incorporating a classical spin Hamiltonian successfully replicated the magnetic phase diagram and its intricacies. This theoretical model demonstrates that the unique features of this material can be understood through the complex interplay of geometric frustration and lattice asymmetry.

The task of allocating non-divisible goods to self-interested agents in a competitive environment has been extensively studied in economics and game theory. Our investigation extends this research by exploring specific fairness principles applied to calculating allocations. We are particularly interested in determining whether mechanisms exist that yield pure Nash equilibria and ensure that fair allocations are met. This inquiry leads us to the concept of $k$-fair mechanisms, which demand that every pure Nash equilibrium lead to an allocation meeting the standards of $k$-fairness. We analyze two types of $k$-fair allocations: those with $k$-fair Christian social welfare and those with $k$-fair Envy-Free properties. We establish that, in scenarios where goods and agents possess identical properties, the VCG mechanism always results in pure Nash equilibria and conforms to the standards of Christian social welfare or Envy-Free allocation. Moreover, we identify specific $k$-fair allocation types, including those with $k$-fair Christian social welfare or Envy-Free properties, for which we guarantee the existence of pure Nash equilibria through the design of mechanisms based on the Guo and Liu (2019) approach to combinatorial auctions. However, we also prove that, in scenarios where goods and agents possess differing properties, no mechanism will ever yield pure Nash equilibria for Christian social welfare allocations requiring positive values. Our exploration of fair allocations through the lens of self-interested agents' strategic interactions may serve as a

In our research, we diverge from the standard practice in unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) of employing a direct one-to-one correlation ('mapping') between source and target domains. Instead, we utilize stochastic translations to account for the inherent ambiguities in domain transformations. This strategy enables us to achieve better results by generating various outputs based on a single source image, thereby increasing the likelihood of accurately predicting corresponding target images. We utilize novel translation models that incorporate conditioning on the labels and use them to develop two main models: the ambiguous one-to-one mapping model and the ambiguous multi-mapping model. Our experiments demonstrate that incorporating target domain noise and using label conditioning on the target side significantly boost performance. Our models set new records on the adaptation of natural domains and excel in the challenging domain-to-sketch scenario, outperforming previous studies.

UGC 8839, an exceptionally faint spiral galaxy, is characterized by minimal star formation except in its central region. A comprehensive study of this galaxy using radio data with the EVLA and optical data with the CFHT, reveals that UGC 8839 possesses a remarkably stable disk with low star formation rates. Observations indicate that UGC 8839's spiral structure is highly ordered, with distinct and symmetrical arms. Furthermore, a detailed analysis of gas and stellar components shows that UGC 8839's disk is a self-gravitating system in equilibrium. Contrary to general spiral galaxy trends, UGC 8839 exhibits low gas masses in its central region, and a peculiar offset between its gas and stellar centers. A comprehensive exploration of possible causes for its low star formation rates, including interactions with nearby galaxies, reveals no concrete evidence of such events. Nonetheless, a brief radio source, host-ing a low-power black hole, is present in UGC 8839's central region, and may contribute to its elevated star formation levels.

Researchers propose using paleo-detectors, an experimental technique, to detect dark matter. Unlike conventional detectors, which require massive and expensive set-ups, paleo-detectors utilize naturally occurring rocks with deep geological history that contain tiny damage tracks from dark matter interactions. Thanks to advancements in microscopy and the ability to study samples over billions of years, paleo-detectors can potentially offer more sensitive detection at significantly lower costs. This could significantly expand the range of sensitivity in dark matter research. Using updated analytical methods, scientists have simulated the capabilities of paleo-detectors under various conditions and found them robust against inaccuracies in age measurements and the composition of samples. Even with relatively high concentrations of radioactive contaminants, the sensitivity of paleo-detectors can surpass current limits, offering the possibility to detect dark matter interactions below existing detection thresholds, even when masses are less than ten GeV.

This paper introduces a novel form of leakage in modern encrypted databases, specifically 'update pattern leakage'. A formalized definition and security framework for DP-Sync are presented, leveraging differential privacy through 'DP update patterns'. A proposed framework, DP-Sync, builds upon existing database schemes by incorporating differential privacy-protected update patterns, ensuring the entire update history of outsourced data remains confidential.

The extensive use of Machine Learning (ML) in high-security sectors necessitates a transparent understanding of its methodology. Nonetheless, research into decoding ML models like Random Forest is in its nascent stages. To bridge this knowledge gap, we employ rigorous mathematical techniques and logical reasoning to create a pioneering method for explaining the predictions made by Random Forest. Our approach revolves around Minimal Unsatisfiable Cores and furnishes an exhaustive analysis for feature importance, encompassing both localized and broad aspects, along with adversarial sample examination. Empirical results across multiple datasets showcase the precision of our feature importance assessments. Furthermore, our method outperforms the current state-of-the-art adversarial analysis technique and offers the ability to generate user-centric reports that can inform recommendations in real-world scenarios.

Minimally invasive surgery has emerged as a highly effective treatment, allowing for non-invasive exploration of abdominal organs. Advances in medical technology, particularly high-definition cameras and sophisticated software, have enhanced its efficacy and paved the way for computer-assisted procedures. Although the process still faces technical challenges, we have investigated several popular deep learning approaches to improve automated detection and tracking of surgical instruments during laparoscopic surgery. The evaluation of our methods revealed that a novel deep learning network outperformed existing alternatives, yielding impressive accuracy and real-time processing capabilities. The exceptional performance of the model, characterized by low error rate and fast frame processing, shows great potential to support and optimize the efficacy of laparoscopic surgery.

Current public datasets for re-identifying individuals are limited due to the difficulties associated with labeling them. Despite the abundance of unlabeled surveillance footage that can be utilized for training, a significant bottleneck exists in expanding existing re-identification datasets through manual labeling. One possible solution to address this challenge is to train a re-identification model in an unsupervised manner using surveillance footage that is already available. In this paper, we propose an unsupervised training approach centered on contrastive learning, allowing the model to distinguish between identical individuals and dissimilar non-matching individuals. Moreover, we employ cluster K-Means to segment person identities based on the extracted features, effectively expanding the dataset through soft labeling. Our model, trained on an unsupervised dataset comprising approximately 200,000 person identities, demonstrates superior performance when evaluated on both benchmark supervised datasets, outperforming top-validated models, and real-world evaluation trials, surpassing current state-of-the-art models in real-world scenarios.

This paper presents an original model that uses a unique threshold measurement formula in the Realized-GARCH model. The new framework utilizes a non-linear model that takes into account the 'leverage effect' and models the connection between realized volatility and hidden volatility. A specific estimation method was adopted, a simulation test was performed to evaluate its effectiveness. Furthermore, the paper conducts a practical study using real-world data, predicting Value-at-Risk and Expected Shortfall for various stock market indices with different confidence levels. Results show an improvement in forecasting accuracy compared to traditional GARCH and Realized-GARCH type models.

Recent findings from global pulsar timing arrays data suggest a nano-Hertz gravitational wave background signal, but current research lacks a comprehensive understanding of the uncertainties associated with individual low-frequency ridges in the data.  To address this knowledge gap, a new statistical approach called the Bayesian Information Criterion is proposed for selectively thinning pulsar timing arrays data and estimating the uncertainty associated with low-frequency ridges.  Utilizing a simulated dataset of 32 pulsars, the proposed method is tested and compared to a widely adopted power spectral density estimation technique.  The results show that the new method is more robust in estimating the uncertainties associated with low-frequency ridges.

Using lattice QCD, a lattice calculation for the correlation function of two quark currents within a pion has been performed. The results were derived in a manner suitable for the extraction of chiral distribution functions of the pion. The findings were compared with theoretical predictions made using the bootstrap boundary value approach and the effective field theory approach. The study revealed that the quark momentum distribution functions within the pion exhibit momentum dependence that aligns with lattice QCD calculations, whereas the x-space distribution functions, when calculated using lattice impulse approximation potentials, were found to be overestimated by the theoretical predictions made using the bootstrap approach. Furthermore, the comparison with impulse approximation potentials provided insight into the Kroll-Rosa relation, confirming it holds accurate up to x=0.5.

Evaluating protoplanetary disk evolution is closely tied to understanding how
mass accretion rates are influenced by a star and its disk properties.
However, accurately using observed relations in this context is hampered by
not properly accounting for variations in mass accretion rates, a problem
especially prevalent in earlier stages of star formation.  Analyzing new and
existing observations, the variability of XX Cha is shown for the first time
to be highly variable over a few days in a pattern not linked to regular
exoplanet orbital periods.  This kind of large-scale variability, when factored
in to typical life-span observations, significantly narrows the range of all
possible mass accretion rates, a finding that challenges existing relations
between mass accretion rates and stellar properties in order to be valid.
Consequently, new relations for mass accretion rates must be developed for
better understanding how mass accretion varies and affects the formation of a
system's planetary architecture.

This study explores how uncertainty about chance influencing job success and earnings impacts redistribution policies in a diverse group of people. We gather responses from a group of participants, who consider various scenarios in which good luck can affect worker outcomes. The results show that participants generally want to reduce the gap in earnings, but are less motivated to do so and exhibit smaller differences in income inequality when chance plays a role. These findings have implications for research aiming to measure the perceived impact of luck on earnings and the desired level of income inequality redistribution.

Removing a subspace from a partial flag results in another partial flag consisting of fewer components. This action induces a mapping $\pi : X \to X'$ between corresponding flag varieties, which essentially discards information to yield a coarser partial flag structure in $X'$. In a context of stable maps, for sufficiently large degrees, a key geometric object - associated with maps that target Schubert varieties $X_i$ - exhibits the structure of a rational connection over its parameter space in $X'$, which now reflects maps targeting $\pi(X_i)$. Furthermore, this discovery links quantum $K$-correlators to specific values, which we then show extends to an equivariant framework. By examining a universal hyperplane arrangement $Fl_{1,n-1}$ and the behavior of maps onto it, we are also able to identify relationships in its quantum $K$-ring through a geometric, analytical approach that includes Chevalley's theorem.

The development of modern machine learning applications is centered on data and is complicated by a critical issue - understanding the influence of data quality on training. The problem lies in isolating the effect of data quality from other variables affecting the model's performance. To tackle this challenge, a novel approach is introduced that utilizes the Shapley value to assess the importance of training data on model accuracy. To calculate this, a mathematical framework is developed that accounts for the interdependencies between data quality and model biases. The approach is demonstrated through a series of experiments, involving the simulation of noisy data and real-world datasets, showing its effectiveness in identifying high-bias data samples. The code and the proposed formula are presented as potential foundations for future research on data importance analysis.

We investigated possible connections between the number of radio sources observed within 22 galaxy clusters from the MAVERIC survey, and factors such as collision rates among stars within those clusters ($\Gamma$) and their masses ($M$). Our data showed no correlation with collision rates, but revealed an increasing radio source count with greater cluster mass. This pattern may indicate that more massive clusters have more prominent intermediate mass globular clusters capable of hosting persistent radio sources, especially if such clusters tend to have smaller black hole-to-star mass ratios, thus producing more radio emitters through low-luminosity accretion.

We investigate a widespread challenge in analyzing complex graph systems: many real-world networks are more effectively modeled as hypergraphs, yet their associated datasets are often presented as projected graphs. To better comprehend this phenomenon, we establish a theoretical framework to examine its underlying principles and worst-case scenarios. This framework facilitates the identification of specific conditions that dictate whether a graph's inherent hypergraph structure can be accurately recovered through supervised graph learning approaches. Our studies also reveal that certain irrecoverable instances may resemble certain real-world graph databases, implying that our results can provide valuable insights for graph analytics applications involving hypergraph data.

We propose an advanced concept for measuring directional emission in microcavity lasers. Initially, entropy in the polar far-field profile effectively gauges the degree of unidirectional light release, outperforming previous methods which struggle with variation. Secondly, we introduce a phenomenological angle for measuring emission directionality, but its practical application is limited to straightforward cases due to the inability to handle complex structures. Conversely, entropy based on semi-marginal probability in the Cartesian coordinate achieves comparable results and is also adaptable to emissions with complex structures.

The scattering of coherent light from heated alkali metals in a range of 350-450 Kelvin is examined in detail, and atomic spacings are measured in terms of wavelength from approximately 0.7 lambda to 0.1 lambda. A comprehensive theoretical framework models thermal alkali metals as groups of interacting radiating dipoles, and demonstrates that photon correlation data can be accurately predicted through random atomic pair positioning. Experiments confirm our findings with positive outcomes. Adjusting key variables within these experiments offers opportunities to investigate distinct regimes of photon behavior.

Offline learning for multiple interacting agents is crucial for developing
practical applications involving multiple interacting entities. Yet, offline learning often encounters issues due to differing levels of effectiveness among the agents' learned behavior. For example, if one agent has a random policy while the others are more skilled, existing offline methods can lead to compromised performance overall. To tackle this problem, we present a novel offline learning framework called Shared Individual Trajectories (SIT) that explicitly considers the diversity of individual trajectories. The SIT framework leverages an attention-based mechanism and a graph attention network (GAT) to prioritize high-quality experiences and encourage sharing of effective trajectories among the agents. Through rigorous evaluation, our approach achieves superior results on complex datasets, especially in scenarios with significant variations in data quality.

We developed a novel approach for registering MV images, utilizing a Convolutional Neural Network, in both 2D and 3D. Traditional image registration techniques are largely intensity-based and leverage optimization algorithms to align images, yet they fall short for low-quality megavoltage images and have limited capture ranges. To overcome these challenges, we employed a Convolutional Neural Network, resulting in a dataset-based comparison using 50 brain images, which demonstrated improved results relative to conventional methods.

In 1927, Einstein used the Solvay conference to pose a fundamental question regarding the completeness of the quantum theory. He employed a thought-provoking scenario involving the entanglement of two spinless particles in separate locations to illustrate the concept of wave function nonlocality. We would like to utilize this well-known example to clarify the concept of single-particle entanglement and demonstrate its implications. By examining the particle's behavior in various scenarios, we demonstrate that entanglement of separate particles is a direct consequence of single-particle entanglement. Furthermore, we prove that particle entanglement can lead to the phenomenon of particle steering, which represents a nonlocal effect that cannot be achieved through local operations alone. Additionally, we show that the quantum correlation between two particles, often referred to as quantum nonlocality, arises solely from the single-particle entanglement of these particles.

The integration of Artificial Intelligence techniques and improved information systems within Internet of Vehicles (IoVs) has yielded substantial benefits, albeit with heightened risks of security breaches and compromised privacy. As IoVs technology continues to evolve, there's growing interest in privacy preservation methodologies that adapt to these changes. Federated Learning has shown promise in safeguarding IoVs data and addressing concerns about security and privacy, whereas Blockchain technology presents possibilities for secure and verifiable data management. This paper conducts an in-depth review of Blockchain-Enabled Federated Learning frameworks for IoVs, exploring potential problems, viable solutions, and future directions. This comprehensive survey can serve as a foundation for developing novel BC-Enabled FL solutions to address various IoVs data privacy challenges and scenarios.

V392 Persei, classified as a dwarf nova that underwent a classic nova explosion in 2018, is an extraordinary object whose extreme evolution over nearly three years has been closely observed.  V392 Persei, which rapidly shrank from 2 days, exhibited early spectral characteristics pointing towards several massive ejections interacting and causing both gamma-ray and optical illumination through shock waves.  V392 Persei entered its most brilliant phase about 200 days into its eruption, as massive ejecta finally overtook its inner white dwarf layer.  Although the classical nova shell of V392 Persei has begun to display signs of growing, the extraordinary object still holds many secrets in understanding the complex and unpredictable phenomena of small binary star explosions.

In quantum computing, generating the entanglement of any number of qubits in a single operation has significant implications for error correction, particularly when combined with stabilizer measurements. Utilizing a single multi-qubit gate instead of several two-qubit gates in parity-check circuits is demonstrated using the toric code, resulting in improved fault tolerance when applying a five-qubit gate over individual two-qubit gates in the context of quantum error correction, particularly when applied to ion qubits susceptible to spontaneous photon scattering, leading to an approximate $40\%$ threshold advantage in the latter case.

A proposed precoder codebook and feedback encoding approach leverages Gaussian mixture models (GMMs) to construct codebooks and reduce information exchange between base station and mobile terminal. Initially, the base station trains a GMM using uplink signal samples, then creates a codebook based on GMM components, assigning one entry per component. Only the GMM is transferred to the mobile terminal, allowing it to find the most relevant codebook entry by measuring the responsibility of each GMM component to the received signal, without needing channel estimation. Feedback is transmitted as the index of the most responsible component and corresponding codebook entry, leading to enhanced performance over traditional approaches, notably in scenarios with limited pilot data transmission.

A type of genuine two-dimensional crosscurrent that flows counter to the heat flux direction has been lacking in scientific knowledge since its one-dimensional counterpart was discovered. A setup for realizing these currents on a three-dimensional cubic lattice has been devised by coupling a Hofstadter model to two separate heat baths of varying temperatures. Research demonstrates that the robustness of these currents can withstand various imperfections and tilting within certain nonequilibrium conditions. Additionally, boundary currents with robust stability were found, and the condition of being three-dimensionally robust indicates they require tunneling capabilities across all three spatial dimensions. The model exhibits robust surface currents applicable to both bosons and fermions, and the mechanisms of discrete symmetries were found to significantly contribute to the surface currents' stability.

For asymptotically flat spacetimes, where light is emitted at a distance from the gravitational source, research indicates that the Bondi mass aspect must satisfy specific requirements to reach the point of infinity without obstruction. In general relativity, such constraints result in an upper limit on the mass change rate in relation to the speed of light and gravitational constant, leading to an interesting insight into Dyson's maximum luminosity theorem. In contrast, the conditions under which scalar gravitational waves in Brans-Dicke theory allow light to escape infinity without being overpowered by rapid mass loss.

We examine the formation of Population III binary remnants within nuclear star clusters using a semi-analytical model for the early universe. Our framework accounts for the movement of Population III binary remnants during the formation of the universe's structure and identifies which of these remnants fall into nuclear star clusters through gravitational interaction with field stars. Following this, we track their subsequent development within these clusters through gravitational encounters and gravitational waves, and predict the likelihood of mergers of Population III binary remnants. Our study shows that about 12% to 20% of Population III binary remnants fall into nuclear star clusters and that between 1.6% to 2.5% of these will merge within a nuclear star cluster over the current 10 billion year period. However, if we only consider clusters similar to the Milky Way's GC, we find that between 0.4% to 0.6% of Population III binary remnants will merge within these clusters over the same time period. Our predicted rates of merger that result in black hole formations range from 0.08 to 0.24 per billion years for all nuclear star clusters in the universe, and from 0.02 to 0.08 per billion years for clusters similar to the Milky Way's GC. These rates could be high enough to significantly account for the LIGO/VIRGO's detected events like S190521b.

A portable Gamma-Ray Burst simulator has been developed for the Gravitational wave High-energy Electromagnetic Counterpart All-sky Monitor. This simulator simulates Gamma-Ray Bursts using a Lithium-drift detector and a resistive anode encoder, and its performance is evaluated with results showing it is capable of detecting and analyzing GRB signals similar to those of GECAM's Keithley and RAE detectors.

This article investigates the semigroups of composition operators on BMOA-type spaces, specifically on BMOA_p and its analogue VMOA_p. BMOA_p is a part of the family of F(p,q,s) spaces introduced by R. Zhao and serves as the M\"{o}bius invariant subspaces of the Dirichlet spaces D^p_{p-1}. Our focus lies in analyzing the maximal subspace of strong continuity for semigroups of operators, exploring sufficient and necessary conditions on the infinitesimal generator of phi for the semigroup [phi_t, BMOA_p] to equal VMOA_p. We also establish the connection between the maximal subspace of strong continuity and the Volterra-type operators T_g, specifically examining which symbols g make T_g bounded or compact from BMOA to BMOA_1, while also investigating the relationship between compactness and weak compactness of T_g on BMOA_p when 1 < p < 2.

Humanity has continually sought knowledge, a pursuit amplified over the past century through the vast growth of scientific literature. However, despite employing metrics such as citation counts and impact factors, it remains unclear how a discipline's knowledge amount correlates with productivity, specifically how the value of new knowledge varies over time. In our study, we introduce a method to quantitatively assess the evolution of scientific knowledge within each field and across all disciplines, ultimately enabling the distillation of vast literature amounts into reduced summaries of decreasing quality over time. Our results reveal the uneven distribution of new knowledge production, with some fields quickly overwhelming researchers with new information and others requiring more time to do so. Additionally, we uncover substantial gaps in knowledge that have yet to be formally documented, especially in disciplines outside the core, as identified by influential citation tracks like ArXiv, ChemRxiv, and Physics World. Our approach may also be applied to monitor the spread of misinformation, research productivity, and the preservation of cultural heritage through literature and art.

In this study, we examine the security risks associated with wireless communication systems that use dual hop OFDM technology. To mitigate this issue, we analyze two main cases: one involving a single user with a single relay, and another with multiple users and relays. The primary goal of this investigation is to determine optimal power allocation methods across various frequencies in order to enhance end-to-end data transmission security while adhering to power consumption constraints at both the sender and relay nodes. By utilizing high signal-to-noise ratio approximations and optimization techniques, we can develop effective power allocation methods that prioritize system security while minimizing bit error rates and ensuring that physical layer requirements are met. Furthermore, a multi-user case is investigated to demonstrate the superiority of proposed solutions over conventional approaches that fail to consider the unique characteristics of physical layers. Successful implementation of these methods is validated through simulated results using MATLAB software.

Two-dimensional systems with robust edge currents due to large Chern numbers offer a wealth of chiral modes related to their topological invariants. In photonic configurations, these edge currents translate to stable multi-mode waveguides that naturally protect the topological properties of the system. In our research, we combine these photonic setups with quantum sources, using a Harper-Hofstadter model to illustrate scenarios where quantum emitters display nearly quantized emission rates. These increased emission rates can result from interactions with multiple edge modes within different energy gaps. Notably, we find that spontaneous emission from these sources can separate spatially, creating time-bin entangled states upon applying a single control pulse. Furthermore, we explore the possibility of emitters selectively interacting with distinct channels via light-matter coupling. These capabilities provide the foundation for implementing quantum operations among topologically protected modes, ultimately enabling the development of robust, two-dimensional quantum circuits protecting error-prone quantum information through symmetry-protected phases.

In the complex context of an urban intersection with automated and human-driven vehicles, we explore an essential challenge: generating safe pathways for automated vehicles. Our research focuses on preventing rear-end collisions when a connected vehicle's human-driven leader approaches the yellow and red phases of the traffic light. We've developed a predictive control system that can instantly forecast how the preceding human driver operates and utilize this prediction to create a safety-oriented pathway in a limited timeframe. The performance of this framework has been tested using a simulation and we assess its reliability.

Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 300 actions per second, largely because of outdated technology used to create them.
Our research presents TextWorldExpress, a highly optimized version of three widely used text-based game challenges, achieving a remarkable increase in simulation processing speed of roughly three orders of magnitude.
On ordinary computer hardware, it can process over one million actions per second, allowing for extensive tests lasting merely a day rather than weeks or even months.

Deep learning models such as Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) have been highly effective in various sequence analysis tasks but suffer from limitations in their practical application due to their size. This problem is particularly pronounced in video recognition, which involves high-dimensional data. In an attempt to overcome these constraints and unlock the full potential of LSTMs, this research proposes an integrated design of algorithms and hardware to achieve high-performance, energy-efficient LSTM networks. At the algorithmic level, a new LSTM structure called FDHT-LSTM is developed, which significantly reduces model complexity without sacrificing accuracy. In addition to this optimized algorithm, a customized hardware platform is also designed to efficiently execute the FDHT-LSTM model by incorporating a sophisticated memory access scheme that minimizes data conflicts and allows for real-time matrix transformations. Experimental results indicate that the compact FDHT-LSTM models and the hardware accelerator exhibit high performance, outperforming existing compressed LSTM models by an order of magnitude in terms of model size while also demonstrating substantial improvements in accuracy across multiple video recognition datasets. Furthermore, the proposed FDHT-LSTM architecture is found to excel over a leading tensor decomposed hardware model called TIE in terms of model size, latency, and energy consumption in various benchmark tests.

Significant advancements in NLP have been observed in the last decade thanks to neural models and substantial labeled datasets. However, NLP models are often hindered by a reliance on extensive data availability, hindering their application to resource-constrained settings and unique tasks necessitating large-scale labeling. As a means of enhancing NLP data efficiency, data augmentation techniques have been investigated in recent years. A systematic examination of data augmentation in NLP under low-labeled data settings has been lacking until now, resulting in difficulty in comprehending the efficacy of diverse methods in various contexts. This study provides a comprehensive survey of data augmentation in NLP under low-labeled data settings, encompassing an overview of methods such as token-level and sentence-level augmentations, along with experiments conducted on 11 datasets across topics news, discourse, and text classification according to the CoNLL-Doc standard. Our research enables the formulation of guidelines to aid in the selection of suitable augmentations based on the nature of the data and the characteristics of the model. Our findings demonstrate the superiority of structured and semi-supervised data augmentation over control and unstructured methods, alongside the superiority of transformer-based models over RNN-based models in augmented datasets.

The concept of the Weak Gravity Conjecture is often expressed through its effect on the mass-to-charge ratio of a particle. Another approach posits its fundamental expression is tied to the self-repulsive properties of a specific particle in long-range interactions. A new, closely related formulation suggests it could be formulated in terms of a particle's charge-to-self-repulsion coefficient, which we find is inherently positive-definite and thus implicitly encapsulates the principles of the Conjecture. Building on this framework, we also derive a condition for the convexity of a charged operator in a Conformal Field Theory, which we observe is in line with the spirit of the Conjecture. Notably, this convexity requirement is not universally satisfied by all CFTs, as we see by examining an example of a CFT affiliated with an infinite series of extended supergravity theories, where we find that convexity is violated at specific points corresponding to black holes and certain types of branes.

To stabilize the estimation of ground and excited states on a quantum computer, we modify the quantum imaginary time evolution (QITE) to utilize the model space. This model-space QITE method iteratively expands the model space while maintaining its orthogonality, enabling simultaneous description of multiple states. We enhance model-space QITE by integrating the quantum Lanczos algorithm, which boosts its convergence rate. In simulations, our approach outperforms both standard quantum Lanczos and the folded-spectrum QITE in calculating excited states. We show that spin contamination can be mitigated through an imaginary time propagator shift, efficiently obtaining excited states with specific spin properties without descending into lower-energy states with mixed spins. Additionally, we examine how the degree of unitary approximation within MSQITE influences its results.

Given a Noetherian local ring with a specific prime characteristic and its primary ideal in terms of an $\mathfrak{m}$-primary parameter, we establish criteria for $F$-rationality based on the tight Hilbert function of that ideal. These criteria make use of a specific polynomial and its coefficient. Additionally, we provide a lower bound for the tight Hilbert function that extends a previous result from Goto and Nakamura, which specifically holds true in equidimensional excellent local rings with a specific prime characteristic.

The rapid transformation of the electricity sector necessitates innovative ancillary services that guarantee the stability and dependability of the electricity network. Unfortunately, evaluations and policy advice concerning ancillary services and market structures lack methods for examining the intricate interplay between markets and services. Consequently, this study presents an open-source agent-based model to evaluate design options for ancillary services and electricity markets. The Ancillary Services Acquisition Model incorporates a comprehensive understanding of grid stability and electricity market mechanisms to simulate the behavior of generators, transmission system operators, and sometimes, flexible assets. This model enables the exploration of intricate market interactions and allows for the evaluation of design options for ancillary services and electricity markets.

R.W.K. Odoni initially established the connection between the Galois group of an iterated polynomial and the symmetric group in fields of characteristic zero. A generalization to fields of positive characteristic was achieved by Juul. Building on these findings, we explore a scenario involving an irreducible polynomial F over the algebraic closure of a finite field k(t) with algebraic and separable coefficients. When a generic monic polynomial Phi is composed with F, resulting in a new polynomial with coefficients (a0, a1,...), we identify the Galois group of the composite polynomial's mth iterate. The structure of this Galois group mirrors the (m-folded) iterated wreath product of the symmetric group S_(nd) for some positive integer n. Notably, when n=1, this relationship aligns with Odoni's and Juul's earlier work. Moreover, we establish a connection between the Galois group of the mth iterate and the n=1 case after a specific transformation, which effectively folds the symmetric group's structure multiple times.

To study non-resonant Higgs boson pair production in the $\textrm{HH} \to \textrm{b}\bar{\textrm{b}}\textrm{W}\textrm{W}^{*}$ channel at the LHC using the matrix element method, we examine how to differentiate the Higgs boson pair signal from the dominant irreducible top quark pair background. Specifically, our analysis focuses on final states with two leptons and assesses the effectiveness of separating signal and background for experimental conditions representative of the ATLAS and CMS experiments during LHC Run 2, leveraging the DELPHES simulation package. As a result, we were able to achieve a $0.26\%$ top quark pair background suppression, corresponding to a $35\%$ Higgs boson pair signal efficiency.

We calculate one-loop corrections to the Standard Model process of a Z boson emitting a Higgs boson, considering extended scalar sector scenarios for the Standard Model, including inert doublets and various triplets, quintuplets, and septuplets with different new scalar SU(2)L representations. These new scenarios are expected to be probed at a precision of a part in 10^4 through precision studies of the Standard Model. Specifically, we find that for the extended scalar sector scenarios under consideration, new interactions between the H and Z bosons and the physical Higgs boson can lead to a deviation of up to -6.7 in 10^4 in the value of a certain precision quantity, and this effect can reach as high as -13.6 in 10^4 when considering the lightest inert doublet model. Furthermore, we show that the precision that can be achieved through precision studies of the Standard Model process of a Z boson emitting a Higgs boson will provide valuable constraints on the parameters of the lightest inert doublet model, potentially improving existing bounds on this scenario by a factor of five to ten. Additionally, we find that the effect on the Higgs boson self-coupling from these scenarios will be from negative one hundredth to positive one hundredth, and that the scenarios under consideration will also impact the process of a Standard Model Z boson decaying into two photons, resulting in a potential shift in the value of this precision quantity

Saturn's polar atmosphere is significantly influenced by seasonal changes, with mid-latitude jet streams that hinder the development of persistent polar low-pressure systems. Research on Saturn's polar atmosphere is ongoing, but it is largely based on observations of Saturn's southern pole. This study is the first to investigate Saturn's northern polar atmosphere during the planet's summer using data from the Gemini North telescope and the Atacama Millimeter/meter-wave Observatory. It discovered a persistent cold polar vortex in the northern hemisphere's summer and tracked its development over several seasons. The vortex formed about two Earth years after Saturn's summer began and had characteristics similar to those of the persistent vortex in Saturn's southern pole. It also found a persistent cold area in the northern hemisphere's summer, surrounding the vortex, and tracked the vortex's development over a full astronomical year. This cold area, a hexagonal shape, appeared about one Earth year after Saturn's summer began and had temperatures about 1 degree Kelvin lower than surrounding areas. It is not clear what caused this feature or why it is not present in the southern hemisphere's summer.

This paper investigates solutions to the Schrödinger equation under the influence of a focusing nonlinearity with mass-supercritical properties, in a domain exterior to a compact convex obstacle in a higher-dimensional space. We demonstrate that solutions with negative energy will inevitably collapse within a finite time period. Additionally, under the assumption that the nonlinearity is not too strongly energy-dependent and given specific symmetry conditions, we find that solutions with zero energy will collapse within a finite time period. Both of these outcomes can be derived from an approach improving upon previous work of Holmer and Roudenko, requiring minor modifications to handle higher-dimensional space scenarios.

Note: Our approach builds upon their method employing almost compact solutions within almost straddled spaces, though we've made significant enhancements, including establishing almost orthogonality within almost intermediate spaces, thereby relaxing the condition of exact orthogonality required by Holmer and Roudenko.

We provide a novel proof that local characteristic-zero, semi-parametric embeddings for a polynomial variety defined over the integers have an equivalent form to local positive-characteristic reductions of the variety for nearly all prime numbers.

The manner in which the surface of materials is terminated has significant implications for their physical characteristics. Investigating the metal-insulator transition in V$_2$O$_3$ films necessitates a deep comprehension of the effect of surface termination.  Our studies using X-ray absorption spectroscopy and high-resolution photoemission spectroscopy, carried out on V$_2$O$_3$ films prepared using the double-step method and showing large variations in thickness, revealed that the surface termination is not uniform below a critical thickness of 6 layers.  This discovery allows us to rule out layer thickness variations as a contributing factor to the metal-insulator transition observed in V$_2$O$_3$ films.  Instead, we find that average layer thickness plays a crucial role, with the critical thickness for the metal-insulator transition located at 4 layers, a distance much shorter than the spatial extension of the d-orbitals in V$^{3+}$.  We propose an 'atomic-scale island model' to better explain how the metal-insulator transition occurs at the surface of V$_2$O$_3$ films.

Our study uncovers new features of non-equilibrium double dark-soliton configurations for a quantum Bose gas in one-dimensional space. We find a specific scaling behavior in the condensate fraction as we change the size of the system. This new finding allows us to determine the exact average density of non-condensate quanta. In addition, we identify a specific scaling for the one-body density matrix and a particular rotation for it that represents a quasi-local quasisoliton operator. This new understanding is based on a specific Bethe ansatz approach.

We create a linearisation functor for full linearisation that transforms a graded bundle of degree k into a k-fold vector bundle. Our analysis defines the image of the full linearisation functor, resulting in a subcategory of k-fold vector bundles. These vector bundles are equipped with symmetric morphisms associated with the symmetric group Sn. A significant observation arises in the degree 2 scenario, where this added structure leads to the concept of symplectic double vector bundles. These have an opposite relationship with metric double vector bundles. The process of full linearisation is also used to extend N-manifolds and a superising method for a graded bundle.

This informal discussion begins with an exploration of certain integral expressions involving orbital integrals from the work of Langlands-Shahidi. We compute initial key measures, including $N_{G_{\phi}}^{*} d_{\phi}$ and $N_{G_{\phi}}^{**} d_{\phi}$. Our analysis focuses particularly on measures for which $N_{G_{\phi}}^{*}$ and $N_{G_{\phi}}^{**}$ are inverses of one another, a property we find to be a measure of these integrals being well-behaved. We note that several of the measures we compute fit this criterion. Next, we establish relationships between certain standard measures, including $dx$ on $G_{\phi}$, $d_{\phi}$ on $G_{\phi}$, and $N_{G_{\phi}} d_{\phi}$, a type of normalization we find useful. We also examine relationships between different normalized measures computed using different measures for integration, a process we find involves transformations of the initial measures. Ultimately, we find that computing the geometric part of certain orbital integrals can be a matter of computing the geometric part of an integral of a function over $G_{\phi}$ with respect to $dx$.

The interaction between light and matter is used in various spectroscopic techniques to extract details about a sample's molecular, atomic, or nuclear components. Although scattered light conveys both amplitude and phase information, this phase information is frequently lost during standard intensity measurements, yet it is crucial for reconstructing essential details of a target, as evident from applications like coherent x-ray imaging. A new algorithm is introduced that allows for retrieving phase information from two-dimensional time- and energy-resolved spectra, a feature we demonstrate with x-ray scattering off M\"ossbauer nuclei using a synchrotron radiation source. The knowledge gained through phase information also leads to accurate reconstruction of energy spectra from experimental data, a level of precision that cannot be achieved with other methods. Our approach provides a useful data analysis tool, offering a beneficial impact on x-ray quantum optics and M\"ossbauer spectroscopy that employs synchrotron radiation.

By linking quantum error correcting codes to models of disordered classical statistical mechanics and examining the phase diagram of these models, researchers have found a valuable tool for studying how these codes resist errors under various noise conditions. This study expands this mapping to account for realistic faulty quantum circuits when describing quantum error correcting codes. First, based on a detailed circuit noise model, we develop a strongly correlated classical spin model corresponding to each circuit noise scenario. This approach is illustrated using the quantum repetition code, where we simulate the impact of periodically malfunctioning stabilizer readout circuits. We utilize Monte Carlo simulations to investigate the phase diagram resulting from these interactions, and our findings are compared with the performance of a minimum-weight perfect matching decoder. This research provides a method for assessing the fundamental error thresholds of quantum error correcting codes, independently of any specific decoding strategies, and could help improve the design of near-term quantum computing hardware by identifying the critical noise levels that these codes can tolerate.

Recent theoretical predictions stating that group VI elemental monolayers can't be in the form of a honeycomb lattice structure have been disputed by new experimental findings. In this study, it's been found that incorporating oxygen into these monolayers, specifically tellurene, makes them dynamically stable in both experimental and computational analyses. A specific functional group, COF, is then used to perturb the system in a way that increases its stability. By using first-principles calculations, our findings show that the functionalized tellurene layer has a very large gap of around 0.36 eV, along with non-trivial Z2 topological properties. This makes it a suitable candidate for being a large-gap 2D topological insulator, particularly for the production of stable Hg-wires. Our predicted values for the energy gap of this system also align with recent experimental measurements of work function changes, providing strong evidence for our theoretical findings.

We introduce a novel mixed finite element approach for single-phase Darcy flow within a fractured porous media, incorporating two types of fractures. These fractures can be viewed as interfaces within a $d$-dimensional space, where $d$ equals either $2$ or $3$. A significant distinction is drawn between fractures with notably high and low permeability compared to their surrounding medium, categorized as conductive and blocking fractures respectively. Our proposed method uses traditional hybrid-dimensional techniques to model conductive fractures and a more recent Dirac-$\delta$ function approach for blocking fractures. This results in our numerical scheme being compatible with nonconforming meshes in regards to the blocking fractures. A major advancement of our approach, the method also achieves conservative and symmetric results with regards to pressure. Successful testing of our approach has been conducted against established benchmark cases, utilizing both analytical and computational methods to validate its effectiveness.

A comprehensive examination of a spin-triplet superconducting device, which involves a spiral magnetic arrangement, is conducted. The underlying metal exhibits unique magnetic characteristics, established through experimental and theoretical analysis, and its effectiveness is demonstrated through a simple model. Further, our research reveals that a spiral magnetic arrangement can function as both a spin-valve and a lateral spin-valve device. This novel structure utilizes a unique mechanism, where a change in the spiral magnetic arrangement causes a variation in the long-range magnetic order, resulting in distinct effects on superconducting electrons' spin and spatial distribution. Consequently, this leads to an asymmetry in the device's behavior, and this asymmetry can be modulated by adjusting the spiral magnetic arrangement. Additionally, this device's functionality can be controlled through an applied external magnetic field, which facilitates the realization of a lateral spin-valve effect. A key advantage of this device is that only a relatively weak external magnetic field is required, and it exhibits a unique persistence of effect upon removal of the external magnetic field. A related issue, concerning the metal's magnetic characteristics being influenced by an applied external magnetic field, is addressed, and it is shown that a small amount of magnetic disorder does not significantly impede the device's functionality.

Hypothesis evaluation plays a significant role in cognitive science, where Bayes factors can compare and contrast competing theories by assessing their consistency with available data. However, implementing Bayes factor analysis is often complicated and heavily dependent on the accuracy of computational methods and Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) samplers. These challenges are exacerbated across multiple model comparisons, a scenario common in cognitive science research. In an effort to facilitate reliable Bayes factor computation, we tested the efficacy of several workflows, including distinct MCMC samplers, data pre-processing techniques, and model specification formats, using a case study that analyzed visual recognition memory. Our findings indicated that using bridged MCMC samplers, a standard notation for model specifications, and a straightforward data pre-processing approach yielded the most precise results, supporting the feasibility of performing Bayes factor analysis with a level of robustness and reliability that can be achieved without prior expertise in statistical computing.

Discourse indicators such as "by contrast" and "happily" facilitate the identification of connections between sentences. To improve the effectiveness of sentence representations in classification tasks, research has been done on predicting these indicators between sentences. This work diverges from this approach by using a trained model to forecast suitable indicators between sentences that have an established semantic connection, based on existing research on predicting indicators. A tool called DiscSense has been developed to perform this task and facilitate research in this area. To assess its capabilities, DiscSense was used to evaluate various aspects of discourse indicators, including (1) the relationship between semantic relations and discourse indicators, (1) the choice of indicators depending on sentence order, and (3) the relationship between parts-of-speech and indicators.

We investigate the properties of a negatively charged nitrogen-vacancy center in diamond under high-temperature and vacuum conditions.  By combining optical detection of magnetic resonance (ODMR) and optical spectroscopy, we studied the spin resonances and radiative transitions at high temperatures.  Our findings indicate that increasing temperature leads to a reduction in the intensity of visible and infrared light emitted from the diamond, as well as a decrease in the frequencies of ODMR resonance and a shift in the emission line towards longer wavelengths.  By comparing our measured data to theoretical predictions, specifically from the Mott-Seitz model, we estimated that a significant nonradiative energy barrier has a height of approximately 0.24 electron volts.

The backpropagation algorithm, though effective for training neural networks, has a significant drawback: it mandates the sharing of weights. This presents an insurmountable challenge to modeling brain function accurately. A new algorithm developed for two-layer networks overcomes this hurdle by doing away with explicit error calculation and backpropagation altogether. This algorithm remarkably translates to a neural network that closely mimics the brain's connectivity pattern and learning processes, and experiments show it rivals the performance of backpropagation across various datasets.

Using field-theoretic methods, researchers studied a spin model on the triangular lattice, where the SU(3) representation was placed on each site, mimicking an antiferromagnetic Heisenberg spin model with p-box symmetry. Taking a large-p limit, they found the model reduces to a relativistic sigma model in three-dimensional space, described by the SU(3)/U(1)^2 manifold. Through a semi-classical expansion, they obtained an effective action and analyzed its topological properties, revealing gapless modes protected by symmetry and a non-zero topological Chern number that characterize the model's bulk and edge behavior. Comparing theoretical results to numerical data, researchers found a substantial p-dependence, influencing the formation of quantum spin-liquid phases. Furthermore, they discovered that certain parameters corresponding to p values of 2 and 6 exhibit magnetic instability in the sigma-model framework, supporting previous DMRG findings.

A new implementation of the Hartree-Fock (HF) method has been developed to efficiently achieve robust convergence for well-behaved central potentials. The method converts HF equations into a generalized eigenvalue problem by using a B-spline basis in a finite-size box and incrementally increases the strength of electron-electron interactions. The accuracy and performance of this implementation were verified through a series of tests, including calculations for atoms and ions using the Coulomb potential, electron gas models with various shapes and sizes, and alkali-metal clusters modeled with a soft-shoulder potential. The findings from these tests were used to investigate the parameters that affect computational efficiency and the choice of electron density. Furthermore, a comparison was made between results obtained with this implementation and those from established methods for atoms and ions, electron gas models, and small alkali-metal clusters.

The distinction between orderly and chaotic behavior within complex networks of interdependent oscillators corresponds to varying functional states found in numerous applications, including active brain states and stable electrical grids. Researchers have a longstanding interest in identifying the categories of dynamic states that these highly responsive systems can exhibit. A recent study distinguished the distinct states by determining the determinants of explosive synchronization – a highly sensitive phase where chaotic behavior suddenly gives way to orderly activity. The analysis indicates that explosive synchronization occurs when a specific critical relationship is met, namely when the difference between an oscillator's individual frequency and that of the overall population falls below a certain threshold. The discovered criterion provides a foundational tool for a more in-depth exploration of the complex phenomena present in these systems, potentially leading to a comprehensive classification of the different functional states that these systems can exhibit.

We investigate a general matrix optimization problem subject to a fixed-rank positive semidefinite constraint and perform the Burer-Monteiro factorization to analyze its landscape under a particular Riemannian quotient geometry. Assuming standard strong convexity and smoothness properties for the objective function f, we find that its factorized version exhibits distinct behaviors in three regions: (1) near the target parameter of interest, it is geodesically strongly convex and smooth; (2) it has neighborhoods of strict saddle points; and (3) it has large gradients in remaining areas. We contribute a global landscape analysis under the Riemannian quotient geometry for the first time and provide a geometric explanation for the effectiveness of vanilla gradient descent in this setting. When f satisfies a weaker convexity property, we discover a geometrically distinct phase of strict saddle points. Our results demonstrate that convexity is the primary driving force behind the geodesic convexity of the factorization landscape.

A graph's edge coloring can be described as assigning different colors to edges based on a specific distance criterion, effectively mirroring the requirements of a certain vertex coloring in a transformed version of the graph. This notion was initially proposed as an open problem by Faudree, Schelp, Gyárfás, and Tuza in 1990, assuming a 4-color solution for all bipartite graphs of high enough girth. We present a 3-color counterexample to this assumption with the graph G being a bipartite graph of girth 4, constructed by taking two large enough complete subgraphs of 1000 vertices and combining them with 1300 edges.

Let $q\ge 3$ be an integer, with $\chi$ denoting a Dirichlet character modulo $q$ and $L(s,\chi)$ being the associated Dirichlet L-functions. This paper will present specific function series, along with novel identities linking the L-functions with Gauss sums, particularly focusing on identities related to $L(2,\chi)$.

High-energy particles with masses beyond TeV range are difficult to access with existing and foreseen particle accelerators.  A novel, high-energy particle physics experiment is proposed to be located on board a next-generation astronomical satellite, capable of detecting the highest energy particles ever observed.  A proposed new experiment combines astronomical observations with particle physics principles, offering a chance to explore an uncharted energy spectrum.  The proposed experiment, involving a telescope array on board a satellite, aims to find rare, high-energy particle events associated with gamma-ray bursts and other extreme astronomical events.  The proposed experiment has the potential to find new, fundamental physics phenomena, such as new, very heavy particles with masses up to EeV range, breaking existing theoretical parity assumptions, or new, long-lived particles that could provide evidence for extra dimensions.  The proposed experiment also considers the possibility of new, very heavy particles with masses up to EeV range that could provide evidence for new, very long-lived particles with masses up to EeV range that could provide evidence for new, very long-lived particles with masses up to EeV range that could provide evidence for new, very long-lived particles with masses up to EeV range that could provide evidence for new, very long-lived particles with masses up to EeV range that could provide evidence for new, very long-lived particles with masses up to EeV range that could provide evidence for new, very long-lived particles with masses up to EeV range that

Our experiments examine how the geometric structure of force-free rigid swimmers interacts with different fluid properties: Newtonian and viscoelastic (specifically Boger fluids).  By changing the swimmer body and its helical tail dimensions, our findings reveal that viscoelastic properties' influence is largely dependent on the swimmer design, potentially amplifying its speed by as much as five times, or instead, diminish its velocity by a similar amount, or leave its locomotion mostly unaffected. Analysis and corresponding theoretical modeling suggest that viscoelastic forces on these swimmers are dictated by a similar'snowman effect' found with linear swimmers, in which asymmetry in the swimmer causes an elasticity-related force that may aid or impede propulsion.

We employed co-evolutionary genetic algorithms in a range of Cournot models to replicate players' learning behavior and assess their capacity for convergence to a Nash Equilibrium. Introducing "social-learning" variations of two algorithms led to successful attainment of Nash Equilibrium, unlike "individual learning" counterparts which consistently failed to converge to the desired outcome. Utilizing simulation outcomes with a specific approach as well as general statistical analysis, our findings showed that "social" learning versions resulted in an ergodic Markov Chain, characterized by frequent occurrence of states leading to NE play in the stationary distribution. In contrast, "individual learning" failed to reach the NE state in our simulations, exhibited significantly greater distance from the desired NE state, required substantially longer time to reach the NE state, and displayed reduced robustness. Ultimately, our results confirmed that the majority of games reached a Nash Equilibrium when players used the "social" learning algorithms.

The growing threat landscape in cybersecurity demands increased vigilance, 
wherein existing vulnerability information can be utilized to enhance knowledge 
and predictive analytics for risk mitigation. By structuring security 
knowledge as an ontology, we can automate vulnerability detection and 
analysis. However, current vulnerability databases are often incomplete, 
missing information about software vulnerabilities extracted from text. 
We propose a deep learning approach to enrich security ontologies with 
entity relationships and their respective proof points by mining unstructured 
text from security forums, blogs, and news articles. Our model, a Stack 
Bi-directional Encoder Transducer, is designed to entwine the understanding 
and generation of language for entity relation extraction. We further 
demonstrate the efficacy of this approach by enhancing the securityQA 
ontology using entity relation extraction and incorporating 10K entities 
from various domains into securityQA. Formally defining entities, 
relationships, and their corresponding proof points as concepts, axioms, and 
instances, we successfully transformed 18K text documents into 10K 
entities, encompassing 179 distinct relations and their accompanying 
proof points, thereby significantly enhancing the comprehensiveness of the 
securityQA ontology. We have made securityQA-ER, our entity relation 
extraction model, along with the enriched securityQA ontology, publicly 
accessible for further security knowledge base expansion.

Doping an Ising model into a nonequilibrium situation, specifically on a complete graph, results in a novel Ising-doped voter model that exhibits both ferromagnetic ordering and spontaneous symmetry breaking at a critical point, despite being influenced by random flips that counter magnetic alignment. The effects of doping are explored in relation to the Ising universality class in both the equilibrium and nonequilibrium domains. Doping acts as a catalyst that facilitates the system's transition into a ordered state and speeds up the critical exponent of the correlation length in both scenarios. Furthermore, the system exhibits a unique coexistence of magnetic ordering and polarization due to the interplay of ferromagnetic interactions and random flips. The influence of temperature, ranging from low to high, reveals a correlated disorder that impacts the system's behavior from protecting its symmetry to inducing spontaneous symmetry breaking. The system's phase diagram is fully examined, and a specific ratio of doping to temperature sensitivity defines the boundary of magnetic ordering and polarization.

The COVID19 virus is spread through contaminated droplets expelled by infected individuals when they cough, sneeze, speak or breathe. Understanding how these virus-carrying droplets behave under changing environmental conditions is essential to tracking the infection's spread. To investigate this, we examine the movement of evaporating droplets influenced by gravity and varying weather, observing how they change in size until either settling on the ground or breaking down into small particles that linger in the air. Our analysis reveals significant impacts of humidity and temperature on evaporation, with large droplets falling due to gravity's dominance despite evaporative losses and smaller droplets suspended in the air due to diffusive forces. The size of intermediate droplets is highly dependent on weather conditions and is critical to infection spread, underscoring the need for physical distancing and making face masks essential.

Deep neural networks are fundamentally altering the landscape of how data and physical laws are combined, resolving complex problems in physics and engineering that had proven insurmountable with conventional methods. Nevertheless, evaluating the accuracy of NN-based predictions proves more complicated than traditional methods. This difficulty arises from not only the random fluctuations inherent to noisy data but also limitations imposed by data quantity, model specifications, hyperparameters, optimization techniques, sampling, and overfitting. Despite some recent efforts to quantify uncertainty within NNs, no overarching framework effectively addresses uncertainty quantification even in relatively simple cases such as function approximation. Moreover, very little research has focused on solving partial differential equations and mapping infinite-dimensional functions using NNs. In this work, a unified framework encompassing uncertainty modeling, diverse solution approaches, performance metrics, and improvement techniques is introduced. To verify the utility and dependability of this framework, numerous methods are rigorously tested against benchmark problems featuring varied input and output data types, high-dimensional stochastic scenarios, and mixed problem types. Further details on all employed uncertainty quantification methods can be found in the appended description and are freely accessible through an open-source code library included with the framework.
